speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: U.S. UNDERGROUND TEST-REQUEST FOR INTERNATIONAL SUPERVISION
speechtext: I should like to ask a question of the Prime Minister. Will the government consider making representations to the government of the United States that, if that government is to undertake an underground atomic test explosion, as reported, this should be done under international supervision, having regard to the fact that its results might help resolve the major technical issue now standing in the way of agreement on a test ban, namely the possibility of detecting and identifying small underground explosions?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: U.S. UNDERGROUND TEST-REQUEST FOR INTERNATIONAL SUPERVISION
speechtext:
This suggestion is similar to one made by the Leader of the Opposition some weeks ago. At that time the Leader of the Opposition was informed that the suggestion was a very interesting one and that study and consideration would be given to it.
That is the position at the moment. There is not any immediate necessity for a final determination in this connection. The idea advanced by the hon. gentleman is similar to that advanced by others recently, and is certainly worthy of serious consideration.

subtopic: U.S. UNDERGROUND TEST-REQUEST FOR INTERNATIONAL SUPERVISION
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. Can the Prime Minister say whether consideration of this same laudable suggestion is being given in so far as it might affect any explosion in the Athabaska tar sands?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: U.S. UNDERGROUND TEST-REQUEST FOR INTERNATIONAL SUPERVISION
speechtext: In so far as an explosion in the Athabaska tar sands is concerned, I think it is some two years ago that I spoke on this matter and pointed out that while it was desirable that there should be a suspension of tests, those tests whose purpose was the advancement of the general good should for civil purposes be excepted. In taking that stand, of course, there is nothing to deny the necessity of every consideration being given to the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition, and that statement would be equally applicable to the question now asked by the hon. member for Assiniboia.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS BY CANADIAN WELFARE COUNCIL RESPECTING REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 3 the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked me a question relative to the representations made by the Canadian Welfare Council. The question appears in Hansard for March 3 last, at page 1683. In answer thereto I set out the several representations which were made by the welfare council. Subsequently on March 10 the hon. gentleman asked me again about this matter, and I shall now deal with the several questions inherent in the interrogation made by him.
I would advise that, in respect of the various recommendations made, each is receiving consideration by the appropriate department. The recommendation with respect to the expansion of the plan to bring in additional families on the same basis as the 100 tuberculosis cases has already received an answer from the Secretary of State for External Affairs on March 2, and the necessary arrangements are now under way.
Then there were recommendations with reference to sponsorship. The Canadian government has not limited the sponsorship to refugees who are in camps. However, I should point out in that connection that the United Nations high commissioner for refugees has on several occasions expressed the wish that refugee camps would be cleared out during world refugee year, which indeed is the primary objective of the high commissioner for refugees.
In the case of sponsors who apply for refugees after the end of world refugee year, which will conclude on June 30, such applications will receive the same consideration as those given during world refugee year, for as the house knows Canada's policy has been to encourage the admission of refugees.
As was recently stated by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, 2,800 refugees were admitted to Canada during the calendar year 1959, of which 1,400 were admitted during the first six months of world refugee year.
There was a further recommendation regarding measures to provide for the legal adoption of refugee children. It should be pointed out that the laws of adoption in Canada are matters of provincial jurisdiction, and in any case the United Nations high commissioner for refugees has informed us that no refugee orphan children in Europe are available for adoption.

I think that is as far as I can properly go at this time, since action on these various recommendations will require extensive consultation with the refugee agencies abroad and with the provincial and municipal authorities.

maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS BY CANADIAN WELFARE COUNCIL RESPECTING REFUGEES
speechtext: I take it the Prime Minister is not able at this time to say anything about the recommendation with respect to medical care?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS BY CANADIAN WELFARE COUNCIL RESPECTING REFUGEES
speechtext: No; that is right.

The farm security act in Saskatchewan, Mr. Chairman, provides security to farmers in their homes, security against eviction. This type of security has been repugnant to the federal government; therefore, as I understand it, the provincial government is to introduce or has introduced amendments to remove the provincial protection that has been given to farmers on a comprehensive base, and remove its application so far as this act is concerned.

The information I have-and I do not vouch for its accuracy; that is why I am asking the question-would indicate that very few loans of this type have been made in Alberta and Saskatchewan. I therefore think it is fair to ask what the exact figures are, back for two or three years, shall we say, for the amount of loans that have been made to farmers in Alberta and Manitoba. Then we can judge to what degree the 100,000 farm families in Saskatchewan have been deprived of beneficial legislation by the provincial farm security act.

I have here some correspondence-and I am quite prepared to send it to the minister for his perusal when I sit down-which points out that a certain company, a mortgagee under the National Housing Act, namely the Investors Syndicate of Canada Limited in the city of Edmonton, Alberta, has rejected a fire insurance policy in the name of Cooperative Fire and Casualty Company. I was wondering if the minister had given consideration to some remarks I made in this debate yesterday, when I presented to him the position of the small towns of this country. I think this is a favourable time to ask the minister what may be available to the house builders in these towns as a result of the legislation which is before us, the increased money that may be available for direct loans. I see that the minister has before him not only the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation but a gentleman who used to have supervision in connection with housing loans for the territory that I represent here. I refer to Mr. Hignett.
As a practical exercise, could the minister indicate to me what is likely to result for the individual person say in Kenora, or Fort Frances, or Dryden, or Atikokan, who is anxious to build a house for himself, if we should pass this legislation and provide these funds? We have no big building projects such as they have in the cities, and a great part of this debate has been taken up by the consideration of housing problems on a large multiple basis for the big cities.
I am genuinely concerned, when I hear that the minister has in mind spending about half of what was spent last year in direct loans, about the effect of this change on the small communities of our land, and I wonder if the minister would tell us his conception of what a borrower, say in the town of Kenora or Fort Frances, is likely to be faced with if we pass this legislation, in the light of the ideas the minister has in mind and the policy envisaged for the year ahead.
Since I made a few remarks yesterday I have carried out inquiries, and I find there are almost 5,000 branches of chartered banks in this country. As 1 said yesterday, in so far as recognizing them as approved lenders is concerned we must put them out of the picture. They are not in the picture at all because it is well known, as the minister reported, that in the past month only nine loans have been made from this source.
Faced with such a situation, what is the minister going to do? I personally have been in this house long enough and have been associated with housing problems long enough to know that an attempt was made in the past to encourage the other types of approved lenders for whom a larger interest rate has been provided; insurance companies and mortgage companies, for example. I found that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation did its best in those days to meet this

situation by appoaching these institutions and saying, "You have a social obligation to get down to Kenora and Fort Frances and Dryden and Atikokan" and these other communities with which I am familiar, "and take them individually as your area of responsibility."
The housing corporation did that. They said Kenora belongs to the Sun Life Insurance Company; the Great West should take responsibility for the needs of Dryden, and so on. To a degree those companies met this request, but they were losing dollars and cents on every accommodation they made. In connection with a small building project their inspectors had to travel several hundred miles in order to look over the proposition; and in relation to the same amount of money they could lend say in the city of Winnipeg, on the basis of several hundred houses, hon. members can see that the companies could not be enthusiastic about this scheme because they were actually losing money on account of the expense of inspection, supervision and so on in respect to houses located very far from the head office of the corporation. The result was that while they made an effort, we found on analysis that the individual house buyer or prospective house builder was brushed off.
I say we are going to have the most horrible snafu in 1960 if the banks with branches totalling almost 5,000 across this country are out of the housing game this year. I would like the minister to indicate to me, if he accepts as a fact that the banks cannot make loans at the present rates of interest, what a citizen in Kenora, Fort Frances or these other places is likely to be faced with if he wants to build a home in 1960. Does he have to go to the banks that are not likely to lend him any money and just get on paper a turndown so he can present that to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation as a requisite before the corporation will make him a direct loan?
In addition to that, is it clear that he must be a person whose income is less than $5,000? I would say that the average person in my constituency who is likely to build a home to minimum standards, $10,000 to $14,000, is a person employed in a paper mill, on the railroad or in one of our mines. I would venture to say that only a person whose income is over $5,000 is likely to build a house in 1960 costing in excess of $12,000.
Is the picture as bleak as it seems to me it is for individuals in these small towns, not only in my riding but across Canada?

particularly if he is working on his own account. You cannot ask for his income tax return. If he is employed you could obtain the information from his employer and obtain credit reports on him. The usual methods employed to find out an individual's income will be used here.

If you multiply that by $10,000 a loan, just to get a rough figure, you have an amount of between $140 and $150 million. This year we are planning to loan $150 million to people in this category. speechtext: Yes, except that I think the minister said the 14,239 applications accepted for direct loans were in all income groups?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: I think the minister should indicate how many of those 14,239 loans were made to people with incomes of less than $5,000.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.

speechtext: That is my very point. If you loaned $142 million last year to people in all income groups on a direct loan basis, I suggest to you that if the record shows that only approximately 50 per cent of those had incomes of $5,000 or less you are not giving this committee an accurate forecast when you suggest you may spend $150 million in this category this year. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.

the Minister of Public Works in charge of the activities of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, there will be many people in the income bracket below $5,000 who this year will be applying to us because of their inability to get loans through their banks. Therefore it is to take care of people who want to be able to get loans from their banks that we have made this arrangement. It is a rule we are going to try to work out, and if it does not work out successfully; if, as my hon. friend suggests, we do not get enough applications, I can assure him we will extend the scope so that $150 million will be applied for.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister has still not indicated to me what I regard as something of importance, namely the mechanics that will have to be followed by the individual applicant for a loan in a community such as I have described. He has indicated that he must be turned down by two approved lenders.

speechtext: Not Dryden.

speechtext: Yes; it is 5,500, I think. The minister has his officials in front of him. The information I want is this. National Housing Act
hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River pointed out. subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, obviously the minister is as reconciled as I am to the facts which speak for themselves so eloquently that the banks are out of this picture. subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.

National Housing Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: The next question is, how are you going to find out what their investment income is?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes. The minister told us yesterday that if this bill was passed he would make loans immediately. I should like to know how he would know what people's incomes are?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member for Kootenay West was satisfied. Probably the hon. member for Trinity can never be satisfied. We are going to take the usual credit sources to arrive at a person's income; take a statement from the person, from his employer, and go into the matters in connection with his business and use the usual avenues that a bank manager uses to determine a person's credit rating.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING AGGREGATE AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: That system works not too badly where you are trying to establish a minimum because usually, if you get a statement from the employer, you know what his basic income is, and then he can provide supplementary proof that he is receiving money from investments, which is additional information that the person voluntarily provides. But I have been in business for a considerable number of years and I have seen dozens, in fact hundreds, of those credit reports; and believe me, I would never accept one of those as a maximum of what a person's income would be. I have seen my own, as a matter of fact, and I have seen a number of other people's that I know to be -I would not say grossly-inaccurate; far enough out that they would never suffice for the test the minister needs to apply. How could you possibly determine what a person's outside income is from supplementary sources, from investments or from secondary employment, and so on? Surely, the whole scheme he is putting forward does not make any sense at all unless he can tell us precisely how he intends to do this.

the tests I am now describing. We are well acquainted with the methods of ascertaining what is a person's income. I have outlined the procedure in some detail, perhaps not enough to satisfy the hon. member for Trinity, but enough for most other hon. members of the house.

We lend 90 per cent of the value of the buildings to be erected and the limited dividend owner puts up 10 per cent. This owner can be either a municipality or an individual. We have arranged that the amount will be amortized over a period of 40 or 50 years. We do get our money back. So far on loans we have arranged that we get our money back, and we have done very well. National Housing Act
available to the people who need it most. In this case, the minister has just told us there is no element of government subsidy. This is a governmental service. Surely it should be made available to all Canadians on an equal basis, without discrimination.

Mr. Chairman, since questions are being so readily answered by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), although so far he has been in that position for only six months, I take the liberty of making a few remarks concerning my riding of Beauharnois-Salaberry located south of Montreal in the Chateauguay district. About 1,500 direct or insured loans have been granted in my riding by the C.M.H.C. since the present government came into power. It means that 1,500 new homes were built there in the last three years.
In this respect, I should like to mention the problem of land for building purposes. A few years ago a building lot could be had for three or four cents a square foot, while today builders have trouble finding a property for less than 25, 30 or 35 cents a square foot.
To do a complete job, why could not the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation acquire a few farms, in a given district, so as to control speculators and unbridled speculation? Under such a policy, it would be easier to build low cost houses, within the means of people with average earnings of $3,000 to $5,000. Moreover, the corporation could make this land available to builders who would agree to build only houses costing no more than $10,000, and for which the down payment would be $1,000, all expenses included.
In that way, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, could surely be of great help to families with average or even low income. According to advertisements appearing every day in the big Montreal dailies, the down payment on a house costing about $17,000, is from $2,000 to $4,000, exclusive of other costs that the buyer has to pay.
A man who is required to pay $90 a month over a period of 25 years, in addition to municipal taxes of about $25 a month, cannot meet such a heavy obligation for such a long time, because I do not think there are many people who are assured of the same job and a steady income for 25 years.
If the corporation could help in the purchase of farms as a means of checking wild speculation, which raises serious problems

for municipalities, it would be a great service to people with annual incomes of $3,000, $4,000 and less than $5,000. In that case, people would probably be less reluctant to commit themselves for a period of 25 years because of a lower down payment.
Let us, for instance, take the case of a man who buys a home today in a new municipality and who has to make a down payment of $3,000 cash. If he loses his job or is transferred and has to move and sell his property before he buys another one, he runs into something of a problem, because if he wants to move away as soon as he can, he might have a hard time to find a buyer for his house whose value has gone up, as a result of the monthly payments he has made on it, over and above the down payment.
Many builders claim that it's not simple to do business with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. At the present time the C.M.H.C. offices are rather far between and builders sometimes have to travel 40 or 50 miles when they want to have explanations or details on business procedure with the C.M.H.C.
If municipalities of about 5,000 population or more had a local representative to give talks and tell people how to avail themselves of this legislation, I think people would leave the larger centres, and that more of the smaller municipalities would benefit from this act which, for some years, has been very helpful, especially last year when about 30,000 houses were built through direct loans granted by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
If local inspectors could meet with prospective builders and brief them on the requirements of the act, many people would find it useful, because many builders tell us that in	many cases, by the	time	they areable to	take up	the matter	with	C.M.H.C.officials and find out how to go about securing a	loan, the	summer is	over,	the besttime of	the year	to build is	gone,	and they
have to put off their plans until the following year. And then if, in the meantime, land values go up on account of speculation, those people have to decline the offer and finance their house building with conventional loans.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are the few remarks I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister, and I hope they will prove useful to him.

Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am delighted with the speech made by the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Bruchesi). It was a very good speech, and the ideas he put forward are very interesting; I shall make it my duty to consider them.
I am glad to learn that, in Chateauguay, 1,500 houses were built thanks to the plan we are submitting.
The hon. member has asked whether there was a plan that would allow people to buy low cost land. I am glad to say we do have such a plan. If the hon. member is really interested in the matter, we shall welcome his suggestions, as well as his requests, and very diligently consider any inquiries made of us.
(Text):

On Tuesday evening the
minister, both in the house and on television, attempted to take credit for all the houses that have been built in Canada over the last three years as being the direct result of this government's being in office. I should just like to point out that the figure of 400,000 is not an accurate figure. They are not responsible for 300,000; they are not responsible for 200,000 by any stretch of the imagination. The attempt to read into the record and to put across on television on a national hook-up the idea that 82,000 homes are being built in Canada at the present time as a direct result of the winter works program of the Prime Minister is a real distortion. We cannot help being concerned about the accuracy of the minister's forecast in the light of those remarks.
To summarize our thinking on this legislation may I say that we have tried to point out the inadequacy of the government's housing program for 1960. With the banks now out of the lending field altogether as the result of government action, and with the lending institutions reluctant to tie up substantial funds in long term mortgages, we believe there will be a great need in 1960 for mortgage funds.
With the government's announced intention of cutting in half their lending this year as compared with last year, and with no definite assurance that this half will be lent, the situation will become desperate and housing starts will drop considerably in 1960 unless mortgage funds are found. I believe that at least $200 million should be supplied through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in order to avoid a slump in house 79951-0-137
National Housing Act
building, to distribute more widely the obvious benefits of home ownership, and to provide job opportunities for our unemployed.
I should like to suggest that clause 2 be amended by inserting therein after subsection 1 and before subsection 2 of section 22, the following subsection la;
la. The sum of $200 million of the amount specified under subsection 1, shall be committed for the purpose specified under subsection 1 before January 1, 1961.
Mr. Chairman, as I have said I should like to move the above amendment, but I doubt very much if such an amendment would be in order, desirable though it might be. Therefore it is not my intention to so move; but I do hope that these remarks will focus the attention of the government on this serious problem of the continuing scarcity of mortgage money for home construction in 1960 and underline the need for the most careful attention to this matter on the part of the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 am still concerned with this matter of why we are asking for $500 million when the minister has indicated today he wants to spend only $150 million, although last night he said it might run as high as $175 million. I presume this means that those people in the income group below $5,000 a year are getting the benefit of this estimate to the extent of $150 million. Therefore there must be several aspects of housing legislation to use up the remainder of this amount.
I would ask the minister to explain what other forms of housing legislation he intends to put forward under this particular estimate to use up the balance of this amount. If we want $500 million, I think we should be prepared to spend it. If we are only going to spend $150 million on this low income group below $5,000, then I would like to know why. It may be that the minister has set a minimum on the earnings of people coming under this type of housing, because it is quite obvious that persons earning $2,000, even though they earn less than $5,000, will not be able to build this class of house. Houses in the $12,000 class cannot be built with a minimum income of $2,000 or even less, so therefore there is some new type of housing to be implemented for this kind of person. If that is so, then I would like to ask the minister what it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the answer, very briefly, is this. In 1954 the National Housing Act as we have it now was passed by the former administration. That administration voted at that time to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation an amount not exceeding $250 million. That was done not

National Housing Act
with the idea that the money would be used in any one year; as a matter of fact, after nearly four years only $100 million had been lent.
We are working now on the same principle. We are asking that we should be empowered to lend a total of $500 million more, or to increase the amount which we have already lent from $1 billion to $li billion. They are loans to the corporation from the consolidated revenue fund. This does not mean any more than it did in the case of the former administration. We do not mean to spend it in one year. They did not spend $250 million in nearly four years. We do not know how long it will take to spend it. But it is a mistake, is it not-perhaps the hon. member will agree with this-for us to look into the future and try to calculate with any degree of certainty exactly how much money we will need before we meet here again? Supposing we have occasion to ask for money again. We had no idea this year that it would be delayed until March 17. I am not ascribing any blame to anybody, but nevertheless it has been very embarrassing to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to have this long delay in getting further funds.
As a result of asking in the last few years for just the amount we thought we might need in the immediate future we found ourselves last fall, as the hon. member will recall, in the position where we had enough applications to commit the balance of the $1 billion and we are filling those applications even up to the present time. However, we were forced, by reason of having committed the $1 billion, to cease making further loans, and I think the hon. member will appreciate that in having $500 million added to our funds we are not taking up all the money at this time. We only borrow the money from the government as it is required.
Supposing next year the bill which ordinarily might be put through at this time to increase the amount were not reached until April, or even until this time, in March, we would not be embarrassed again by having committed our funds in advance.
I think that is the explanation the hon. member was asking for. Have I answered that first question, or is there another part?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not blame my hon. friend for not being here all the time. The question I just answered a few minutes ago had been answered three times before, and this answer I have given twice before but I will answer it for the third time.
There is no revolving fund. Nobody appreciates more than my hon. friend, I think, that parliament should remain supreme. Supposing that this money were lent to central mortgage. The return on the principal and interest of all these mortgages would then come back to central mortgage and they would be a very powerful crown corporation clear of any financial responsibility to parliament. Ever since Charles I parliament has been, as my hon. friend knows, very wary of giving up its rights, and the one way to keep an eye on any organization is to make it come to us for money when needed. Therefore parliament controls the purse strings of central mortgage, and all the money which comes back by way of return on principal and interest goes to the Receiver General of Canada to be deposited in the consolidated revenue fund. As time goes on the return will be greater. In 1958 there was paid back to the government by way of principal and interest $71.4 million; in 1959, $85.5 million, and in this year, 1960- we can estimate this with a pretty good degree of accuracy-$110 million.
Does that answer my hon. friend's question?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. While I agree with the history of parliamentary relationship from the time of Charles I, I would think that there is also a relationship between the amount which appears to be growing rapidly of $71.4 million in 1958 and the amount of $110 million in this year. We are asking only for $175 million, so really we are not putting $175 million into central mortgage in fact; we are only putting a little over $60

million of actual taxpayers' money into Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: There is no question that so far we are putting in by way of loans far more money than we are getting back. But we only get our principal back in instalments, plus the interest.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It seems to me that if we project the figures for another two years we would be getting more out of this than we are putting in. It would appear that this year we are getting an estimated amount of $110 million back and that we are spending $160 million, so this government can only claim to be making a contribution of $60 million for housing.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: All the same, of what we got last year for instance, $33.8 million was by way of repayment of principal and $37.8 million by way of interest. It would be interesting to calculate how many years would have to pass before we would be getting back enough money to take care of the total outlay, but that would be a matter for an actuary. If we were to stop lending money right now, or if we could fix a definite amount of future loans, it might be possible to figure it out, but it would be many years yet, I can assure the hon. member.
I wonder if the minister could tell us if there will be any size limitation on houses built by an owner-applicant?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: The hon. member for Trinity will be glad to know that as the result of the limitation placed upon the size of income there will be no continuation of the restriction on the size of the house. This is something which has concerned the hon. member for some time, and he will be pleased to know that the restriction has been removed.

That is very good news, and I appreciate the fact that this change has been made. I made this suggestion in the house last year, and I am gratified that it has been accepted even though it is a year later. I suggest that if the minister would accept the advice tendered to him the year it is given instead of waiting until a year later he would have a very much better policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I appreciate the advice received from the hon. member, and perhaps it is for that reason that the restriction was removed. But I would remind him that I have been in charge of the department for only a year.

We are certainly not holding the hon. gentleman responsible for what happened more than a year ago, as I said the other night. I think this might well be 79951-0-137i
National Housing Act
a proper time for him to consider the removal of this other restriction on income, because I do not think it will work out very well in practice. I think the minister will find that there are an awful lot of Canadians who believe their incomes are no business of Central Mortgage and Housing. I think a lot of them will feel that they are entitled to apply in the same way as other Canadians, notwithstanding what their private incomes may be. Some of the anomalies have already been pointed out-a man may marry a girl with a million dollars and yet be entitled to apply because his own income is $4,900. Another might marry a girl with $20, yet because he is earning $5,010 he would not be entitled to a loan. Loans will not be available to families with incomes just over the permitted figure, and I foresee that all sorts of difficult problems will arise in the administration. This is not equitable, and it is not in accordance with the principles in which we believe. My own feeling is that the minister could find a better way of doing this, a method which would be of more practical use to those responsible for the administration of N.H.A. and of greater benefit to the people of Canada.
As to the removal of the restrictions upon size, I would like briefly to recall some of the difficulties which were raised by the old regulations, because I think difficulties of the same type will arise under the new regulations. It did not work well in the metropolitan areas because, as I said the other day, a lot might cost $5,000 and a house $10,500. The total cost of the house and lot would be about $16,000. An extra hundred square feet of accommodation could be built on a lot for a very small additional cost, say $400; so for an increase of 2| per cent in the total price, the home purchaser could get approximately 10 per cent additional space. This particular limitation was one which did not work in the interest of the Canadian people, and I thank the minister and his officials for having removed it. I think they would be well advised to anticipate the trouble they are likely to have in the administration of the new regulation with regard to the size of income and remove that, too, without waiting for a whole year to pass.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I do not wish to deprive the hon. gentleman of any credit, but the action for which he is claiming credit was in fact recommended before he came into parliament. I do not remember the hon. member being here in 1957.
You were not here.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Yes, I was. I would point out that the regulation did serve a very useful

National Housing Act
purpose, but now the need for it has gone. We were since 1957 trying to serve the ordinary man, and in order to do that we had to put some restriction on the size of houses to prevent houses becoming too big and expensive at the cost of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Now there is no longer any necessity for doing that by restricting the size of houses, because we are regulating it on the basis of borrowing income. Should we find for any reason that this restriction on permitted income is not a satisfactory rule, we may resort once again to the limitation on the size of houses. I appreciate that this does not appeal to the hon. gentleman, because he builds larger houses and is not very interested in houses suitable for those with lower incomes.

I can only say that if it took the government as long to act on the recommendation as the minister has just told us, I hope he will act much more quickly than his predecessor should any new recommendations of positive value be made.
Are local credit unions regarded as approved lenders?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I think the hon. member is a labour union organizer. We have not received any applications so far. When we do, we shall be glad to consider those applications, as we consider all other applications, on their merits.

I certainly hope that the minister will give serious consideration to encouraging the provincial credit union movements to enter this field, because the credit unions are not limited by law to a maximum interest rate of 6 per cent as are the banks, and the difficulty about making loans available to people in the smaller communities might be overcome in part if the credit unions were asked to supply some help to people in meeting their housing needs. By now we have credit unions in thousands of small communities in Canada, and if the chartered banks are unable or unwilling to act and continue to make a major contribution to housing in Canada I would recommend that the possibilities which exist in the evergrowing credit union movement in Canada be explored.
I should like to have a proper understanding as to what took place within the financial field of this whole N.H.A. operation in 1959, and what is the intention of the government this year. As I understood the minister, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation last year spent $340 million on housing in Canada but in that year the Canadian government received $75 million by way of repayments of principal and interest. In other words, the taxpayer had to
IMr. Walker.]
supply additional net money last year for the purpose of housing under C.M.H.C. in the amount of $265 million. In this year the proposal of the minister is that expenditures shall be limited to $175 million under the act in all its aspects, yet the government expects to collect the sum of $110 million by way of repayments of principal and interest.
In other words, only $65 million of new or additional money will be invested in housing this year over and above the amount received on loans made in past years. Last year $265 million, this year only $65 million, a 75 per cent reduction in the activities of the taxpayer through the government toward the promotion of housing in Canada. Does the minister consider that to be an adequate amount in view of rents and the cost of homes continuing to rise and in view of the grave unemployment problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am glad the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked that question because I should say we have still to pay out this year, without any new commitments at all, $317 million, plus $23 million, for a total of $340 million. That is the estimate.
Would the minister explain why he still has to pay out $317 million. This is something new to me. What is this all about?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The hon. member will recall that last fall we instituted the Prime Minister's winter program of builders' loans. That is why there are as many as 82,000 homes in process of being built at the present time. There was such a tremendous number of applications we had to make a cut-off and the box office closed. That money still has not been paid out. There remains approximately $200 million to be loaned in 1960. I am glad my hon. friend asked that question because I guess I have not explained that before.
In other words, we still have to pay out $200 million on loans to which we are committed in the year 1960 without taking into consideration any new business which we will accept after today. Does that explain the matter?

Yes, but let me get it completely right. Out of the $500 million we are now being asked to vote there will be taken first of all $200 million to which the government is already committed and in addition the government plans to spend this year the sum total of $175 million. In other words, a grand total of $375 million is expected to be spent out of the $500 million we are voting?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. I thank the hon. member again for questioning this.

His questions are serving to clarify the matter. Of the $1 billion parliament has voted, $200 million has been committed by C.M.H.C. but has not yet been paid out. Therefore in the year 1960, $200 million of the original $1 billion, will be paid out by way of loans and, in addition to that, out of the $500 million that is being voted today, $150 million to $175 million will also be loaned out, making total loans during 1960-
Loaned out but not paid out.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Loaned out, that is right.
Loaned out but not paid out in 1960.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: We hope it will be paid out.
How could it be?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
It is a question of nomenclature. Perhaps the hon. member for Nipissing would permit me to complete my answer to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, but I thank him for his interjection.
In other words, in the year 1960, we will be loaning $370 million, $200 million out of the original sum and $150 million to $175 million out of this sum.
In answer to the hon. member for Nipissing, it may be true that by the end of the year we will not have paid out all the $150 million to $175 million to which we are going to commit ourselves this year.
That is right. You could hardly pay it out when you have a carryover of $200 million from last year. This is another attempt at window dressing, at gilding the lily.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I cannot win. I am damned if I do and damned if I don't. However, this is a good baptism and I am enjoying it.
Let me return to the question asked by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam who seems to be seriously interested in this question and is not merely attempting to confuse a new minister. I confess I feel sorry for myself.
That is why we say this is going to be a substantial year in building. The sum of $200 million which we were committed for by last October will be definitely loaned out. That is included in the 82,000 homes; that is what it is for. In addition to that we hope that most of the $150 million to $175 million which will be borrowed this year will be paid out as well. We hope they will get right along with the building but there is always a carryover.
In reply to the hon. member for Nipissing, let me say that this money will not be paid for a winter program for builders but will be
National Housing Act
put into direct loans for prospective home owners. That constitutes the difference. In other words, we are not waiting until the fall to initiate a winter program to loan this $150 million to $175 million. We are starting tomorrow. Does that satisfactorily explain the situation?

Mr. Chairman, yesterday the minister made reference to the minimum home. Later I asked him if he could provide the number of such homes built in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I wonder if he could provide me with that information now. If the information is difficult to obtain, next week or sometime in the future would satisfy me just as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: I would appreciate a longer opportunity to secure it. It is difficult to obtain the information over night because we do not have a table for that. We have to take the over-all figures and break them down. We do not mind doing it but it does take some time.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has come back to what I call window dressing with respect to the $150 million that may be spent by way of direct loans in the coming year starting tomorrow, or as soon as the legislation is passed. I am not satisfied that $150 million is likely to be spent this year if the loans on a direct loan basis are restricted to people with incomes of $5,000 or less from now on. I say this because the minister reported to the committee that only 14,239 direct loans were made last year to people at all income levels.
When questioned, the minister said that 52 per cent of those had incomes under $5,000. The minister himself was the one who used a rude monetary yardstick; he has been using lots of rude yardsticks here, but he used one of $10,000 as an average, per loan. The minister said that this would amount to $142 million for direct loans last year. If from now on the direct loans are restricted to people who have incomes under $5,000, and last year they were only approximately 50 per cent of those who received direct loans, how does the minister think he will likely expend in the coming year $150 million or more on direct loans for housing.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
I can say to my hon. friend that last year loans were made to people with incomes of less than $5,000 by approved lenders and direct loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to the number of 24,200. For the reasons that I have explained to my hon. friend, I think we will have a demand for our $150 million from that group; but if the public are beginning to

National Housing Act
think they have enough houses, or if the demand falls off, we will always be able to change the yardstick and increase it to $5,500, and then to $6,000. I can assure the hon. member that we will not have any trouble lending the money; we will see to that.

Yes, I think the minister will have some trouble lending $150 million under his income rules if he really wishes to maintain housing at anything like a standard quantity of total housing, and particularly for people with modest incomes, in the forthcoming year. I would suggest to him that he make soon the review, which he assures us he is prepared to do. Let us look to the merit of this $5,000 income cutoff. I hope he will make his review before he comes before the House of Commons again with his estimates of his department because, before the House of Commons prorogues, we would like to have another look at this, since I have some very grave apprehensions about the number of people who will be served if he maintains this limit of direct loans to people who have incomes under $5,000.
The other thing I raised yesterday, and which I do not think the minister has commented on, is the reference which I made to what was done in 1957 by the minister in charge of housing at that time who went to the Minister of Finance and they in turn associating themselves with the governor of the Bank of Canada went to the chartered banks of this country, which, as I said, have almost 5,000 branches across the country in close touch with our people. As a result of this meeting, the governor of the Bank of Canada assured the chartered banks of financial backing, and I quote from page 28 of the Bank of Canada report of 1957:
The Bank of Canada indicated that the total resources of the banks as a group could be expected to increase during 1957 by an amount at least great enough to take care of their disbursements on mortgage loans in that year, so that it would not be necessary for the banks to dispose of other assets in order to maintain a flow of funds for insured housing loans.
Did the minister think yesterday that this has no merit today? In 1957, the $150 million was provided at reasonable rates of interest to prospective home owners in this country. Is the minister consulting the governor of the Bank of Canada with respect to this possibility?

I have another matter I should like to raise. I was very interested in the reply the minister gave to the hon. member for Assiniboia as to the number of houses that had been built in Alberta and in Manitoba. The minister indicated that in each of

the years 1958 and 1959 no houses had been built in rural Manitoba, no farm houses had been built under the auspices of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and in Alberta only half a dozen houses had been built in each of the years 1958 and 1959, that is on the farms of Alberta, through the auspices of this act. Would the minister now care to agree that no houses were built on Saskatchewan farms under the auspices of this act because of reasons other than the existence of the Saskatchewan farm security act?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will answer all the questions at the end, because every time I get up I only invite a lot more questions.

In that case, I have one more comment to make to the minister unless he aggravates us more. I am going to augment only the comment that I have made heretofore about the value of this meeting in 1957 between the governor of the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks, by indicating to the committee that statistics in the bureau of statistics document relating to new residential construction dated December, 1959 clearly demonstrates the value of that meeting. I have indicated that the former meeting took place with the banks, in March of 1957. The new starts in housing in the second quarter of 1957 went from 8,410 in the first quarter to 40,437. I find here that until the second quarter of 1958 the new administration never reached in any quarter new starts to the equivalent of those which had developed as a result of the banks entering into this picture.
In addition to that, I suggest to the minister that while he has had quite a few comments to make so far about the value of the new administration which came in in June, 1957, I think he has overlooked, in so far as housing is concerned, the relationship of new starts and housing development in so far as the change of government is concerned. I have here a copy of the report of the Senate committee on finance, dated June 12, 1958, when the witness was the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Mr. Bates, who is sitting before the minister now, and I quote from page 45 of the evidence of that committee, where he is reported as saying:
The present government's program began last summer:-
I have indicated that in March, 1957, $150 million was made available from private sources. We all know that in August, 1957, $150 million was taken by the new government from Liberal legislation that was available for direct government housing loans. In any event, Mr. Bates said this:

The present government's program began last summer; that is, the announcement was made; and starts were made before Christmas.
In other words, these results of the latter part of 1957 were-and I am supported by the chairman of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation himself-a result of what had been done by the previous administration. I say it is appropriate at the present time for the minister concerned about housing to look after individuals so that they can escape the clutches of interest sharks. I say that he should at the present time call together, through the instrumentality of the governor of the Bank of Canada as was done in the spring of 1957, the chartered bank presidents to try to do something so that the people who are connected with these almost 5000 branches will have some opportunity to obtain housing loans in the immediate future in their own small locality.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make only a few remarks about the bill we are about to pass. The 1957 bill was very welcome in my constituency of Lake St. John, especially in Alma, with its population of 12,500, where more than 300 homes have been built since 1957.
However, it has created a certain problem, and that is why I ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) to seriously consider appointing a local inspector, because if we put those figures alongside those of another province, we see in the C.H.M.C. report that in 1958, 275 houses were built in Prince Edward Island, whereas in the city of Alma alone there were 327. With the 45 others built in Naudville and 30 more at Isle Maligne, we find that for an urban population of
22,000	people, there were as many houses built as in all Prince Edward Island. And yet we always have to wait for the inspector's report, since he lives in Chicoutimi, and this delays our contractors in their work.
Since the Lake St. John area is steadily developing, the house may be assured that, as a result of the adoption of this bill, which provides for a sum of 500 million dollars, and of the provincial legislation providing for a 3 per cent refund on all loans, house building will certainly increase, both in my city and throughout the province of Quebec.
At present we have 80 applications pending, and people are waiting for this legislation to go through before they complete their
National Housing Act
homes. If I remember rightly, there were some 30 house starts in Alma during the winter of 1959, and if this bill had been passed earlier, we might have gone ahead completing those houses perhaps last month or early this month.
Again, Mr. Chairman, I would draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the fact that we certainly need a resident inspector in our district.
I commend the department for authorizing the Chicoutimi office to pay our contractors locally, which is a great help to them as far as financing is concerned. I take this opportunity of asking that special attention be given to the choice of contractors, so as to protect the subcontractors, because, at a given time, it is the subcontractor who is financing the contractor, and fairly often, in bankruptcy cases, there is nothing left for the subcontractor.
Once again I am happy to tell this house that in my riding there is a considerable increase in building for 1960, and, on behalf of the people in my riding, I ask the department kindly to appoint a resident inspector to help our contractors.
(Text):
I wonder if the minister could give me an answer to the question I asked yesterday concerning a breakdown by provinces of the money spent since the inception of this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Does the hon. member from St. Denis wish the figures for the direct loans-
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: -the builders' loans, the bank loans, the life insured loans, the approved lenders' loans or what? It will take me an hour or so to read them all.
If the minister has not got my question, [DOT] 1 think his officials must have it. I think I asked for both the insured loans and the direct loans by provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: No, I am sorry, we have not before us that detailed information by provinces. However, I would be glad to get it for the hon. member and have it sent to him.

I should like to mention to
the minister that back in 1958 there was a large difference between the number of dwellings built with the help of the federal government in the province of Quebec as

National Housing Act
compared with the province of Ontario. In the journal, La Presse, I read:

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
That a special committee be appointed to examine all expenditure of public moneys for national defence and all commitments for expenditure for national defence since April 1, 1958, as reported in public accounts, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and in particular what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein, with power to

send for persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses; and that in accordance with standing order 67, the committee shall consist of not more than fifteen (15) members to be designated by the house at a later date.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion calls for the establishment of a special committee to look into the expenditures of the Department of National Defence. As hon. members know, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) announced the intention of the government to recommend this action when he was speaking in the house on January 20 last, when he said, as reported on page 143 of Hansard of that date:
-it is my intention to move the setting up of a special select committee on defence expenditures.
Later on the same day he said:
It will review-
That is the committee.
-the expenditures to the end that the ability, the training and the capability of members in every part of the house may be used for the purpose of examining this most important problem.
On February 5 he made further references to the committee when replying to a question asked by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). On that occasion the Prime Minister said, as reported on page 773 of Hansard of that date:
This committee is not to be set up to consider policy. Its function will be to consider expenditures.
The Prime Minister has, I think, made it quite clear therefore that the committee is not being set up to consider policy.
Under our constitutional system of government, decisions concerning defence policy must remain the responsibility of the government of the day, and such responsibility cannot be delegated. There is a great deal of evidence to support that contention, and I might quote an extract from a speech made by the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent when he was prime minister of Canada and was speaking to a motion moved by the opposition of the day to set up various types of committees. On February 1, 1951, as reported on page 28 of Hansard, when referring to the fact that the government is responsible for defence policy, he said, in part:
-that is the way in which constitutional government is carried out under traditional British practice. The government takes the responsibility, under that practice, of formulating policy and of exposing it to parliament. If parliament is not satisfied, then it is the privilege of parliament to dismiss that government and to get a different one.
Later on during the course of the same speech he said:
-full information as to how every cent of every dollar appropriated for national defence is being expended-

And might be investigated by the committee. Then he went on to say on November 13, 1951, as reported at page 971 of Hansard, for that date, when referring to the same committee:
But it would be wrong to think that this committee is being set up to replace the government or to replace parliament in determining the policies of this government in the international atmosphere that exists at the present time.
A little later he said:
It is a committee set up for the purpose of doing what the leaders of the three groups have said to be very essential, that is to see to it that, within the policies recommended by the government and accepted by parliament, the country is getting full value for the appropriations that have been provided.
Finally, in comparing the type of committees which are set up under the British or Canadian system of government with those set up under the United States form of government-and they are quite different in principle-after having referred to what the United States committees undertake in the way of preparing estimates and determining the budget he said, as reported on page 972 of Hansard for November 13, 1951:
Those are matters to be recommended to the house by the government, and to be determined by parliament itself. Parliament having decided what moneys will be available to the Department of National Defence, I believe it is essential that there should be the closest possible check upon the way in which those moneys are expended. I am sure it is the desire of every hon. member in this house to have that money properly expended, and expended in the manner that will produce the greatest possible value for our defence purposes.
Mr. Speaker, those are the conditions under which similar committees to the one now being proposed to be set up have been established in the past. But I may say that despite those limitations I am convinced that salutary results can be expected from an examination of the defence expenditures by this committee.
I can assure the house that any suggestions which will result in economies consistent with policy will be appreciated. They will be appreciated by myself, and I hope we will be able to take cognizance of them and to benefit by the suggestions which are made. Those which are of advantage to the services and indicate economies within the policy of the government will be acted upon in much the same way as the recommendations of the committee on estimates of two years ago have been acted upon in bringing about certain changes of benefit in the administration of the Department of National Defence.
This motion as defined in the orders of the day sets out that the committee is to report its operations and, in particular, to report upon what, if any, economies consistent with
National Defence Committee the execution of the policy decided by the government may be affected. I feel, therefore, that in order that the committee may be conversant with the policy which has been followed by the government it is necessary for me to outline for the benefit of the house the defence policy which has been followed in the past.
I believe that this will meet the wishes of the opposition, because they have for some time indicated that they would welcome the opportunity to discuss defence policies. I notice in the Ottawa Citizen yesterday that a reporter indicated that the opposition was experiencing a feeling of frustration because they had not had an opportunity this session to inquire into defence policies except for casual questions which have been asked from time to time. Really, Mr. Speaker, I did not see any great desire on the part of the opposition to discuss defence policies during the debate on the address, except very briefly, and mainly by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). Nor has the opposition taken any opportunity to move an amendment to the supply motions on this subject. I presume, therefore, that if hon. members opposite are feeling frustrated it may be due partly to their own failure in not having introduced this subject before. Nevertheless, I welcome the opportunity now of explaining the policy which the government has been following in the past in connection with defence matters.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question at this point? I should like to ask the hon. gentleman whether in his remarks he will be initiating a general debate on defence policies, although this particular resolution talks only about expenditure in a given 12-months' period?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: As I said, this resolution confines the committee to the examination of defence spending from the first of April, 1958, I think it is. I am trying to say that since the committee is called upon to consider economies consistent with the policies laid down, I am now about to explain some of the aspects of defence policy in the past in order that the committee might be in a position to realize the basis upon which it might make recommendations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Is the minister suggesting, then, that having stated policy to us, this committee, when set up, will be able to discuss that policy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:

It is a motion to set up a committee, and would not normally introduce a general debate on the defence policies of the government and bring those policies under review and under criticism, thereby constituting a general debate on defence and defence matters.
If the minister intends to proceed on that basis, and the house is content with that, then it is a corollary that the opposition will be free not only to discuss the immediate purpose of setting up the committee but to discuss the defence policies of the government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I may say that our speaker on the subject, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), intends to confine himself to the terms of the resolution precisely. speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
We can be very clear on this: if Your Honour takes the stand that the only question that may be discussed is the setting up of the committee, we are perfectly satisfied. There will be no argument about that. Then we would ask that in dealing with any criticisms which are made thereafter, Your Honour be very strict and maintain the rules to the utmost extent and assure that there be no discussion other than on the setting up of the committee. If that is so, I know the minister will be very willing to discontinue any discussion in so
[Mr. Pearkes.)

far as the policies of the past are concerned, the examination of which will be restricted in the committee within the ambit of this resolution to expenditures and any suggestions for economies consistent with policy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
The reason I rose, as the house will appreciate, is that in looking at this resolution it appears to me that it is like other resolutions to set up a committee, a relatively narrow subject, which would not as it stands open a debate on the defence policies of the government. It would not make those policies the subject of general debate at this time. The issue would be whether it is desirable to set up this committee with these terms of reference.
That was why I rose when the hon. minister began to indicate what course he was going to follow because we must do either one thing or the other. We must debate the motion in accordance with the rules or we must agree that we have a debate on defence policies in general which would open the door to prolonged discussion of the government's policies in a critical vein and an assessment of those policies. Perhaps it is for the minister to say which course he wishes to follow. He can only follow the course of general debate with the consent of the house because it is my duty to restrict it under the rules.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as far as we are concerned we are quite happy if the minister follows the course of initiating a general debate on defence policies. We do that on the understanding that we will have exactly the same right to debate if we care to take advantage of it at this time. We do it also with the knowledge that while the minister may introduce defence policies in this debate the committee that is proposed to be set up will not be able to discuss defence policies.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: That point is not involved at this moment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that point has already been made clear. It is very clear that the committee shall not discuss defence policies. That was made very clear in the debate on the speech from the throne and was also made clear by Mr. St. Laurent at the time the previous committee was set up. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES

National Defence Committee that I made any suggestion.
