As for the examination of expenditures, I ask you to make the most critical examination of those expenditures. There has been nothing wrong in the administration and in the endeavours of my department to save money in every possible way and to expend the moneys during the very difficult times under which they have been working. I think every hon. member knows perfectly well that there is a very distinct change in the whole concept of war at the present time; that we are entering into a new era,


an era in which there are great changes taking place and, therefore, it has been necessary not only for Canada but for every power in the west to follow a policy of great caution in expenditure of money, and many of the projects which were favoured only a few years ago had to be abandoned and changes had to be introduced. Those are the difficult times and the difficult conditions under which we have been struggling for some time in the past. And what help have we got from members on the other side? They have been running all over the country saying we have no policy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Are we not allowed to say that?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I apologize for interrupting the minister again, but we are in this position in this debate. At the beginning, as the minister said, the opposition indicated that it wished to observe the proprieties. The leader of the official opposition who cannot, of course, speak for all of the opposition, indicates that he is not concerned with limiting the debate but, in those circumstances, I ask the minister to observe the rules and not initiate a debate, as he appears to be beginning to do, by discussing policy generally.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The minister, I am sure, is trying to be helpful. He says he wants to meet our wishes in the work of this committee. I wonder whether he would let me ask a question after what he has just said? He has indicated that when his estimates are up for consideration the leader of the house would move at that time that the current estimates be submitted to this particular committee for examination, and he used the phrase "examination of policy". I ask the minister, I ask the leader of the house, if we pass this resolution within those terms of reference, how can that be done?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Bring in another resolution.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: If the minister feels it should be done, why not change the resolution now to make it possible to do it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: One reason that it cannot be changed now, I believe, is that my estimates have not been called yet and they cannot be called until there is a suitable supply motion.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I wonder whether the minister would permit me to raise a point of order? The minister's estimates are before the house; they have been tabled by the Minister of Finance. I am sure Your Honour would agree that it would be quite competent

for the government to change its resolution right now to make it possible, in addition to what is now in the terms of the motion, for the current estimates to be referred at such time as they have been called. I admit they have not been called yet, but they are before the house; all the estimates are, and to empower this committee to receive them at a later date would surely be quite within the rules. If the motion were drafted in that way it would meet the wishes expressed by the Leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are not going to come to a decision by way of anticipation. The house has no right at this time to pass any such motion. The estimates are not before the house in the manner that they require to be in order to permit the course being followed that the minister referred to.
The only motion before the house is the one that is now being discussed. In view of all the circumstances and the fact that there is no unanimity in the house to a discussion beyond the ambit of the motion we are perfectly willing to adhere to the suggestion made by Your Honour that no discussion other than the submission of the motion itself shall be acceptable.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was quite evident before six o'clock that there was no unanimity in the house to a discussion that would permit me to explain what the policy of the government was in order that I might present a background to the expenditures during the period embraced by this motion. I thought I would be in order to do so, and I was somewhat surprised by the attitude of hon. members opposite. I gathered, Mr. Speaker, from your remarks before six o'clock that you were in some doubt as to whether the course I was pursuing was in accordance with the wishes of the house. Subsequent remarks by hon. members opposite would indicate that you were right. In consequence, I shall restrict my remarks directly to the terms of reference of the committee, namely an examination of defence expenditures since April, 1958.
No doubt, Mr. Speaker, you will exercise the same restrictions upon other members. I, therefore, move that concurrence be now given to the motion standing in my name.
National Defence Committee
Hon. L. 5. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, lest there should be any doubt in the mind of any hon. member of this house as to what the attitude of the official opposition was before six o'clock as to the form that the discussion of this resolution should take, let me once more make it quite clear. The minister, apparently, expected to make a statement on government defence policy, and he came here prepared to make such a statement. Speaking on behalf of the official opposition, I made it quite clear that so far as we were concerned we would not object to that but we would expect exactly the same opportunity to talk about defence policy. There was no doubt about this, and the record will show that there was no doubt as to where we stood on the matter.
There is a great doubt, however, in the light of what happened before six o'clock, as to what the government has in mind in proposing this resolution, as to the terms of the resolution as to the limits that are to be placed on the discussion before this proposed committee. Before six o'clock, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes), said this, and I think I am not misquoting him: "The committee"-that is the committee proposed in this resolution which is now before us- "is to make recommendations consistent with the policies which have been established." He went on to say that the discussion of policy, that is defence policy, would not be within the competence of the committee. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) confirmed that interpretation of the function of this committee when he said in his intervention: It is very clear that the committee shall not discuss defence policy.
Then the Minister of National Defence, subsequent to the Prime Minister's intervention, had this to say: "It is my understanding that when my estimates are brought forward the leader of the house will move that they be referred to this committee". This particular committee which, in its terms of reference, is to discuss nothing but these public accounts which have been submitted to it for a particular 12-month period. The minister went on to say that the reference of the estimates-I am sure he was trying to be helpful in making these suggestions to widen the basis of discussion before the proposed committee-would give this committee an opportunity to examine the estimates for the next year and to discuss, therefore, the policy that is to be followed.
The Prime Minister says we cannot discuss defence policy in this committee. The minister says if we refer estimates to this committee we could, in the committee, discuss the policy that is to be followed. If there is, therefore, any confusion in the minds of hon.

National Defence Committee members as to what this committee can or cannot do that confusion has certainly been increased by the statements which were made by the Prime Minister and the minister before six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no confusion here. This committee will carry out a task which is set for it, to examine the expenditures in a certain given period, from April, 1958, and having completed that task then, provided the house approves, the house leader is prepared to submit the coming estimates to this committee. Whenever estimates are submitted, either to a committee or to the house in committee of the whole, policy can always be discussed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I think that is a very interesting and important statement made by the minister, that at this committee, if estimates for the current year or for the coming year are to be submitted to it, defence policy can be discussed.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Do not talk him out of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: No, I will be delighted, if it works. However, the Prime Minister has already talked him out of it by saying that policy cannot be discussed, and I will make quite clear what the Prime Minister has said, not only before six o'clock but earlier.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I am quite certain that if the Leader of the Opposition does not want these estimates submitted to this committee, the leader of the house will not do that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
The submission of the estimates to this committee has nothing whatever to do with the resolution before us. This resolution deals with the submission of the public accounts for the year April, 1958 to April, 1959 to this committee. The government drew up a resolution in these terms and put it on the order paper. We are restricted by the terms of that resolution and when the minister says now that later on the government might do something else which would give us some opportunity for further discussion, how can he expect us not to be confused as to what actually is involved in this resolution?
Let us stick to the resolution we have before us. If later on the government wishes to alter this resolution or alter its policy; if the government wishes to make it possible to discuss defence policy before this or any other committee, that will be fine with us. But that is not within the terms of this resolution. It is not within the terms of what the Prime Minister has said already in this house, as I shall be able to show, I think, without any possible shadow of doubt.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Following what Mr. St. Laurent said.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I will deal with that matter. This resolution has nothing whatever to do with what Mr. St. Laurent said, notwithstanding what the Prime Minister has tried to point out. Anyway, we have this particular resolution before us. The government mountain has laboured now for some time and has produced this mouse of a resolution or, as one member of the press gallery has called it, this runt among committees of parliament. What an apt description of this particular resolution as I shall do my best to show.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Who was that?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: A member of the press gallery.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Let us know who it was.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Yes. I shall be very glad to read it. I have the clipping here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: That is good.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: This very apt description, as it will be my purpose to show, was given by Mr. Tom Gould who is a member of the press gallery.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
The Prime Minister is amused. He asked for it and I will give it to him. Here is what Mr. Gould said about this committee:
This great defence committee is going to be so hamstrung it will never get off the ground.
We shall be able to show that quite easily a little later on. Then he went on to say this:
What the Liberals were after was a committee that could look into the whole foundation of our defence policy; one that could, after hearing professional witnesses, attempt to guide government thinking on the basic philosophy behind our defence expenditures.
They got-
That is, parliament will get it if this resolution passes.
-what must be described as something of a runt among committees of the house.
Lest anyone think that this is the kind of committee we on this side of the house have been asking for, let me go through the record. Before this session of parliament began I made several statements outside of parliament to which the Minister of National Defence has taken apparent exception and said that we should not criticize defence policy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Yes; just before six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
In these statements I pleaded before parliament met in January for the

setting up of a defence committee of this house or for some other mechanism, if the government so desired-a royal commission, if you like-which should go into the whole basis, the whole subject of defence in this changing nuclear age. As the minister pointed out before six o'clock, conditions are changing and those things which may have been appropriate a few years ago for the defence of this country and for the defence of peace may no longer be appropriate. We asked for that kind of an investigation before the house assembled. When the house assembled the first question that was asked by the opposition-the very first question that was asked on January 15 of this year as reported at page 7 of Hansard-was asked by me of the Prime Minister when I said this:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether the government proposes to provide during the present session for an examination of defence policy through the appointment of a small special committee for that purpose.
Not for the examination of defence expenditures which have been made in some past period but for the examination of defence policy at the present time. The Prime Minister replied-and this was on the opening day-as follows:
-when the debate opens on Monday the government's views in general will be discussed, and defence policies will be one of those matters that will be dealt with. In the meantime I suggest that the question remain until Monday, at which time, having regard to press references, I take it, that the hon. gentleman is going to have something to say on this subject.
I had something to say on that Monday. On January 18, in my opening statement in the throne speech debate I asked this question:
Has the time not come to examine from the very foundation our whole defence policy through a small committee-*
Not a defence expenditures committee.
[DOT]-in order to find out where we should be going and how we can best get there, and to work it out if we can on a non-partisan basis so as to do everything we can to make defence policy national policy.
I went on to say this:
It may not be possible to do that. There may be strong differences of opinion and indeed there are at this time-but perhaps a committee of this kind would serve a purpose not only in getting the information before the country but in resolving the differences in parliament in this important matter. A parliamentary standing committee of more than 50 members which has been told by the Prime Minister himself that it must not discuss policy questions is not in my view suitable for this kind of examination.
The Prime Minister intervened at that point and said this:
Does the hon. gentleman suggest that any committee under our system should discuss policy?
National Defence Committee
He has suggested it more than once since that time. My reply was:
It certainly could, Mr. Speaker, if it were set up for this purpose. It could bring in recommendations, get advice on policy and ask the minister about policy questions. It certainly could discuss policy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman read the very next line?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Yes. Then the Prime Minister said:
That is not what Mr. St. Laurent said.
I shall be very glad to deal with that matter. Then the next reference to a committee was made by the Prime Minister in replying to this speech as reported at page 143 of Hansard of January 20. This is what the Prime Minister said on this occasion:
I am therefore going to advise the house that it is my intention to move for the setting up of a special select committee on defence expenditures.
Not even the kind of committee we have mentioned in this resolution which is just a committee to discuss expenditures which have been made. The Prime Minister said on this occasion that he would move that there be set up a special select committee on defence expenditures. Then as reported on the same page he went on to say this:
I am prepared to accept, as is the government, the views of hon. members in this house as to the numbers in that committee, to the end that there will be available a body which will determine the course it will take as to what meetings shall or shall not be open or closed.
What would be the purpose of having a closed meeting to discuss expenditures which have been made in the year that has gone by?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Read the next sentence.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Yes; I shall be glad to read the next sentence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Read it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
It reads as follows:
But in the light of all the circumstances-
This is the Prime Minister speaking.
-it will review the expenditures to the end that the ability, the training and the capacity of members in every part of the house may be used for the purpose of examining this most important problem.
There was no suggestion then by the Prime Minister that this would be sent to the public accounts committee to discuss expenditures that had been made. Surely if he meant anything at all by this statement, and this did not go very far; it did not go as far as to admit that policy matters could be discussed but it did say that current expenditures and current estimates could be discussed; this resolution does not even go so far as that. Then on the same day-

National Defence Committee

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. gentleman? He just made the statement that I had stated that this particular committee would be the public accounts committee. Will he read the resolution? I think he will realize that it states that a special committee be appointed to examine all expenditures of public moneys for national defence and all commitments for expenditures for national defence since April 1, 1958 as reported in the public accounts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I shall be glad to do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I am very happy. Let us get the truth.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Let me quote what the Prime Minister said on the same day, January 20, when I intervened and welcomed the suggestion that there should be a committee to discuss defence policy. Apparently I was a little premature in my optimism because the Prime Minister said as reported on page 144:
I suggest to the hon. member that he did not follow that course in the latter part of his statement. While I appreciate the spirit of co-operation, may I point out the words of qualification which the former prime minister, the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, gave as to the course that such a committee can take under our form of government.
Then later, Mr. Speaker, on March 7, a little more than a week ago, in answer to a question by me the Prime Minister had this to say, as reported on page 1788 of Hansard:
The question as to what is to be discussed in the defence committee is, of course, for the determination of the defence committee, except for the limitation that questions of policy, as the hon. gentleman will agree-
Well, I do not agree.
-having regard to the stand always taken by his colleagues in the last government, are not subjects for consideration by any committee.
In other words, the Prime Minister rests his case on parliamentary experience and practice and convention that considerations of policy are not to be discussed by any committee of the House of Commons. I submit that there is no evidence to support that case.
What have we got in this resolution? The Prime Minister asked me to read it, and I will indeed be glad to do so. The resolution is as follows:
That a special committee be appointed to examine all expenditure of public moneys for national defence and all commitments for expenditure for national defence since April 1, 1958, as reported in public accounts-
I repeat, "all expenditure . . . since April 1, 1958, as reported in public accounts."
-and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and in particular what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein, with power to send for persons,

papers and records and to examine witnesses: and that in accordance with standing order 67, the committee shall consist of not more than fifteen (15) members to be designated by the house at a later date.
This committee envisaged by this resolution is to deal only with expenditure as reported in the public accounts, and the public accounts expenditures go up only until the end of March, 1959.
Does the Prime Minister for one minute think that this committee goes even as far in regard to the examination of expenditures as the committee he suggested on January 20? This investigation stops with the public accounts report, and that puts the cut-off date with regard to the investigation of expenditures at March 31, 1959. This particular resolution would set up a committee which would be even more restricted in its investigation of expenditures than that which the Prime Minister in January said he was going to recommend to the house. It would be completely inadequate for discussion of defence matters. It would be a mockery of any investigation of defence policies and defence questions; if this is the only committee machinery to be set up at this session to go into the whole question of defence.
That is the view taken by practically every newspaper in this country which has ventured to comment, not on this resolution so much as on the earlier statement of the Prime Minister which went further than the committee envisaged in this resolution. Let me quote one or two editorial comments to show how inadequate this committee would be for the purposes we have in mind, and which confirm us in our view that this kind of investigation would be a mockery of the sort of thing we think parliament should be looking into at this very critical stage of defence policy.
The Calgary Herald of January 22, in referring to the Prime Minister's policy statement, said:
Surely the time has come for an honest, thorough bi-partisan effort to face the facts of Canada's defence position squarely and try to arrive at some basis for a policy which will inspire reasonable public confidence.
It goes on:
Such a policy can be determined for external affairs. Such a policy has been undertaken in times of national crisis. Defence today is a crisis of the greatest importance to our security and to our economy.
Then the Montreal Gazette of January 22, in an editorial dealing with the proposal to set up a defence committee on expenditures, indicated one or two of the advantages such a committee might have and went on to say this:
Then comes the third usefulness of such a defence committee. In examining expenditures the committee may open up, not merely to parliament, but

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
to the public the problems, perplexities and purposes of defence in a bewildering age. While this may sharpen criticism, it may also widen understanding.
The Gazette concluded this editorial with the following paragraph:
Government, parliament and people must all know what they are facing. They must have the feeling of facing it together. In proposing a House of Commons defence committee Prime Minister Die-fenbaker will be opening the way to a stronger, not a weaker, defence for this country. For it could lead to a greater feeling of partnership.
So it could if we had the right kind of committee, and we were permitted in that committee to go into the questions of policy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: What questions? Of policy?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Indeed, questions of policy. The Montreal Star had this to say on January 22:
A select parliamentary committee will soon be set up to examine defence expenditures and related topics. That vague phrase "related topics" is used because there is some doubt about how far the committee may pursue its studies. The announcement was hardly out of Mr. Diefenbaker's mouth before the opposition leader was measuring inches in terms of miles. Mr. Pearson said he would be happy to co-operate in working for "national policy on defence on the broadest possible basis."
There was a quick cry of "Whoa!" from the prime ministerial bench. The committee would discuss expenditures, not policy. That was the law that Louis St. Laurent had laid down In 1951 when a similar committee was set up, and he would follow precedent.
The editorial goes on:
Precedent or not, it is a unrealistic limitation to impose on the new committee. There is certainly no argument that the government alone is responsible for defence policy.
And of course, Mr. Speaker, there is no argument about that. The editorial goes on:
To draw a hard line between discussing defence spending and discussing the reasons behind this defence spending would frustrate the potential value of the committee.
Then the Hamilton Spectator had this to say on January 25:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker is in danger of scuttling his own ship and before it is even launched.
Then the Vancouver Sun said this:
Parliament's proposed committee on defence must be allowed to explore government policy on this vital issue. Otherwise there is no point in setting it up.
The Vancouver Province referred to this earlier committee-and that committee would have gone further than this particular committee proposed in this resolution-as "a pitiful substitute". The Prime Minister says that defence policy, or any policy, cannot be discussed by a committee of this house. He takes his stand on the fact, as he puts it,
National Defence Committee that this was the policy of the previous government. The right hon. gentleman has mentioned more than once the committee of 1951 and the attitude of the prime minister of the day, Mr. St. Laurent, toward that committee.
Of course, there can be no possible doubt that responsibility for government policy for defence or for any other aspect of government remains with the government. Nobody questions this under our parliamentary system; nobody on this side is suggesting that we should set up a committee to operate in this field in the way that congressional committees operate in Washington where they do have the power to make recommendations to government which determine government policy, both with regard to expenditure and otherwise. There is no difference of opinion on that score. But there is a very great difference of opinion between us and the government when the Prime Minister says that no committee of this house can discuss, examine or make recommendations on policy, and he will have a very difficult time indeed in supporting that contention from the precedents.
However, that is the argument: the Liberals never allowed it. Even if that argument were a valid one in respect of the past, what an attitude to take now-to say that because the Liberals never allowed it we must never allow it in the future. This is, of course, a stand which is very often taken by the government when they do not wish to do anything. They say: the Liberals did not do it, so why should we do it? Or else: the Liberals did it in one way, and we would not dream of departing from that procedure. Does the government not realize how flattering it is to the previous government to say that because the government of that day did not agree that a committee should be set up to discuss defence policy, this should be an inflexible guide to what should be done in the future? It is a very flattering stand to take to say that everything we did was right, or that everything we refrained from doing was right, and therefore there is no intention to abandon our procedures.
In the same way, the Prime Minister has referred more than once to the precedent of Mr. St. Laurent in setting up the committee in 1951. The resolution in the House of Commons setting up that committee was exactly the same, as the minister or his advisers must know, as the resolution which is on the order paper today, with the exception of one very important change. That earlier resolution did not restrict examination of expenditures to those items reported in the public accounts; that resolution was wider

National Defence Committee in its scope in that it allowed the committee to go into all expenditure, not merely expenditure reported in the public accounts. That resolution in 1951-and this is another contrast between what was done then and what is being done today-was worked out after consultation between the prime minister of that day and the leaders of the other two parties as, indeed, the Prime Minister indicated would be the case on this occasion, although it did not happen. When the leader of the opposition, discussing this particular resolution in 1951, spoke as reported in Hansard on page 955 on November 13, 1951, he had this to say:
I do not propose to discuss the terms of reference because I am satisfied that so long as the committee or the majority of the committee carry forward the intentions expressed by the prime minister the terms of reference will be adequate. I think it is appropriate to say that they are the result of discussions which took place between the prime minister and the leaders of the other parties in the house and myself.
That is how the prime minister of that day worked out, by agreement, a resolution dealing with defence. Mr. St. Laurent said himself as reported on page 972 of November 13, 1951:
They (the other leaders) discussed with me and determined the terms of reference which would provide for a full examination of the expenditures and commitments for expenditure.
Not the commitments in the public accounts report, but the commitments for public defence expenditures generally. That was done following consultation, and when the resolution was introduced into the house, the leader of the opposition of that day was allowed, without anyone raising a point of order, to make a far-reaching and allembracing speech. Mr. St. Laurent also spoke on that occasion.
Today, the Prime Minister has made reference to that speech by taking selected sentences from it, but if the right hon. gentleman would read that speech from beginning to end, as perhaps he has done, such an examination of it will not bear out his contention that there exists any constitutional barrier in our system which would hinder our asking a committee to examine policy and make its views on policy known. When Mr. St. Laurent was speaking on that occasion in 1951 he was speaking throughout in relation to the terms of reference of a particular committee which had been worked out by agreement between the leaders of the three parties. Perhaps the key sentence of his speech on that occasion was this, and I quote from page 971 of Hansard of that year. He said:
But it would be wrong to think that this committee is being set up to replace the government

or to replace parliament in determining the policies of this country in the international atmosphere which exists at the present time.
We agree with that. Mr. St. Laurent was right then, and he would be right today if he were saying that in this house. But this does not mean that a committee of this house cannot discuss policy or that it cannot make recommendations to the government of the day with regard to policy. Indeed, Mr. St. Laurent made that quite clear at the time he was speaking on November 13, 1951. He did object at that time to an extension of the terms of reference of this committee as suggested by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, Mr. Gillis, who wanted to have this committee go into all sorts of related fields such as decentralization of heavy industry. Mr. St. Laurent pointed out that this committee could not do that sort of thing under its terms of reference, but he went on to say that it would be allowed to make recommendations or observations on any matters that might arise out of its investigations.
If anyone should think that a committee of this house cannot make recommendations on policy, that this would be contrary to our British parliamentary practice, as is apparently the view taken by the Prime Minister, what has he to say about a classic case in which such recommendations were, in fact, made? I refer to the occasion when this house set up a joint committee on old age security in 1950. That committee made recommendations to the government of the day in regard to policy, and its recommendations became the basis of government and parliamentary policy. This has been done in the past many times, and it can be done now in regard to national defence if the government so desires.
The right of a committee to discuss policy and make recommendations on policy has many precedents in our parliamentary practice. It even has precedents in this particular parliament. What about the estimates committee in 1958? Did that committee make recommendations to this government on policy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Of course it did.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It did not make recommendations on policy. It made recommendations on administration. Does the hon. member not know the difference between policy and administration?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I will read some of the recommendations made by committees on policy since this government took over. Perhaps I know a little more about this than does my hon. friend the Minister of National

Defence. The minister has suggested that I do not know the difference between recommendations on administration and on policy. Has the minister read the recommendations made by the estimates committee on defence in 1958? I will quote one sentence from that report:
While the committee concurs in the necessity of this expenditure, having regard to the terms of reference, it does not feel authorized to comment at this time on future action with respect to future development of this portion of the defence program. Having made that point, however, and in view of the heavy financial burden, the committee does express its concern in the government entering into any subsequent weapons program of this magnitude-
They were talking about the Arrow program which surely was a question of government policy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I continue:
-without first negotiating for some cost-sharing agreement with either NATO member countries or the United States under the NORAD agreement.
Is that a recommendation regarding government policy?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is expenditure, purely.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I will let the words speak for themselves, Mr. Speaker.
Does the committee on external affairs which has been meeting during this government's term of office-for three years now- make any recommendations of policy? Does it discuss questions of policy? We have been discussing questions of policy in that committee for the last two weeks. Does the Prime Minister suggest that is contrary to British parliamentary practice? If we can do that in the committee on external affairs will the Prime Minister tell me why we cannot do it in the committee on national defence? He cannot tell us because there is no argument for that except that the government does not want us to do it.
What about the committee in 1958 on mines, forests and waters? Read the report of that committee at page 491. Read the recommendations it made. Read the recommendation No. 16 of that committee dealing with the necessity for increased production of coal in this country. Read recommendation No. 17 of that committee dealing with the necessity for greater research by the government. Read recommendation No. 18 advising the government to send a selling mission to the oriental market. Are these matters dealing with government policy in a committee set up by this government? Of course they are, and if it could be done in those committees it could also be done in this committee on national defence if the government were willing to make that possible.
National Defence Committee
Even if this were unprecedented in regard to national defence-and perhaps it is-is that any argument why it should not be done this year? The minister himself said before six o'clock that the circumstances in this country and in the world regarding defence have changed completely in the last few years. Up to 1957 we were following traditional patterns and traditional concepts, as the minister has pointed out more than once, even though we had new weapons. Then about three years ago the whole concept of national defence changed as completely as it changed centuries ago when gunpowder was invented. It changed when the first satellite, the first rocket, went into outer space, and the intercontinental missile became a reality in attack even though defence against it has not yet become a reality.
The minister himself put this very clearly in the debate in the House of Commons on April 1, 1957 as reported at page 2913. I intend to quote his own words. He spoke then not as minister but as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. If this is not adequate justification for an examination of national defence policy, I do not know what more justification could be required. On that occasion the hon. member said:
If we are entering the atomic age, as indeed we are, we must approach the problem of defence from a new angle. There must be an honest searching for the truth. It is now time to take a new look at the jobs to be done and the forces and weapons with which to do them. We need to make a most critical investigation to find out the kind of defence we must have. Other countries are reorganizing their forces, and if our organization requires revamping we should not hesitate to take it in hand.
What are we being asked to do in the committee set up by this resolution? We are being asked to investigate defence expenditures which have already been made. I state that these changes to which the minister has referred and to which I have just referred render many of our defence expenditures at the present time meaningless and indeed a waste of money. Because of that fact I believe that a re-examination in the proper kind of committee of the very basis of defence policy would be valuable to the defence of this country. I do not believe that this kind of examination would be possible in the committee which is envisaged in this resolution.
We visualize a very different committee, one that would discuss defence policy, one that would make recommendations on defence policy, just as the committee on external affairs makes recommendations on a subject very closely related to defence policy which is foreign policy.

National Defence Committee
We visualize a committee which would question the minister on defence policy matters, a committee which when necessary for security reasons-and it would not be necessary very often-would meet in camera; a committee which would not examine serving officers because that is contrary to our parliamentary traditions and I do not think it would be wise to do that, but a committee which could examine experts in the field of defence in this country and outside this country and get their views; a committee which could find out the facts on which policy might be based; a committee which could make recommendations which would help the government in working out future defence policy without interfering in any way with the government's sole responsibility for policy itself.
Another reason why in our view a committee of this kind is essential at the present time is that the statements of spokesmen for the government on defence matters have been so confused and contradictory. I suggest that this confusion and contradiction cannot be cleared up in a committee which is merely going to look into expenditures made in 1958-59.
Take one example as something which might possibly be cleared up in a committee of this kind and which could not even be dealt with by the committee envisaged in this resolution because it is something that has happened since March 31, 1959. I am referring to the use of nuclear weapons by Canadian forces. Whether or not it is a good thing to have nuclear weapons in the possession of Canadian forces is something on which there has been cast every kind of doubt and concerning which there has been every kind of confusion created.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I believe the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) is wandering afar now from the subject under discussion which is the setting up of a committee on national defence. He is referring to statements with regard to policy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think if the hon. member who has the floor pursued that line he would undoubtedly be doing that. I understood him to say that he cited one example by way of illustration and did not intend to follow that line other than to complete the illustration. If that is the case I would not think the hon. member has gone too far.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is well established in our procedure that when we are discussing the setting up of a committee, and when hon. members of this house are
dissatisfied with the terms of the reference of this committee, dissatisfied with the limitations that are imposed on the work of that committee, they can make suggestions as to how the work of that committee should be broadened and as to the subjects that might be submitted to that committee that are impossible in the existing resolution. That has been done on many occasions, especially when we set up the atomic energy committee of this house, when debate on the whole question of atomic energy was permitted.
I am not going to go nearly as far as the leader of the opposition did in 1951, when he was discussing a committee which was embodied in a resolution very much in these terms, but I had hoped that I would be in order in suggesting certain matters which are now in a state of confusion and uncertainty, and I think should be cleared up by examination in a committee but which could not be examined in the particular committee which would be set up by this resolution. One of these matters, of course, is whether we should or should not permit Canadian forces to use nuclear weapons. There are four or five other subjects which I think should go to a committee of this kind which could not be discussed because of the limitation of the resolution and the committee visualized in that resolution. Therefore, I hope I am in order in doing this.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Since the hon. member has asked me I will express my view for his guidance. I do not think it is safe to follow many of the precedents of motions to set up committees because by arrangement the house has often debated the whole subject matter which is referred to a committee. In this case the same choice was suggested but not followed, and we therefore have to consider what rules are appropriate, what are the rules of relevance in a debate of a motion to set up a committee for a specific purpose. It is fair debate, as I see it, to complain about the terms of reference, which the hon. member is doing, and to illustrate his complaint by an example as he has just done; but I would think if he introduced all sorts of examples which were in effect a discussion of defence policy, he would be out of order.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to keep within your ruling. I was suggesting- indeed, I was stating-that under the terms of this resolution there are certain vitally important matters of defence policy which could not be discussed. It is my contention that a committee on defence should be in a position to discuss those matters, whether the Canadian forces, for instance, would or

would not be armed with nuclear weapons, especially as the Minister of National Defence has taken one stand-and an unequivocal one-in this matter and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) has taken another.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: That is not correct. There has been no difference in stands taken. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made the position quite clear as far as the arming of the Canadian defence forces was concerned with nuclear warheads, nuclear weapons. He said very definitely last session and I think again this session that the full potential could not be obtained without the nuclear equipment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes, indeed, that is exactly what the Prime Minister did say and the Minister of National Defence has confirmed that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: No other minister has said anything different.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has given a contrary impression in meetings of the committee on external affairs.
There is another question. The Minister of National Defence said that those weapons-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, please; the Secretary of State for External Affairs would not discuss this matter in the external affairs committee. He said it was a matter to be discussed with the Minister of National Defence.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This is exactly the kind of thing that should be discussed in a committee on defence. There are a good many other things. There is the question of Bomarc missiles that are to replace interceptors, in which there is a great deal of uncertainty and confusion at the present time; indeed, uncertainty as to who is to be responsible for the expenditures on those squadrons of Bomarcs. The minister himself said on March 10, 1959, at page 1776 of Hansard:
Both the Prime Minister and myself have on several occasions stated that there will be two squadrons of Bomarcs ... These will be separate units with complete establishments of personnel, missiles and launching apparatus.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the Leader of the Opposition is now getting into a no-man's-land, if I may put it that way, which I at least had hoped he would not be entering in this debate because I do not think it is relevant.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all I will do is just mention the kind of thing which I think should be discussed, and I am not going into the pros and cons of policy involved in the discussion. What kind of missiles should we
National Defence Committee use? What should be our policy in regard to continental air defence? Should we maintain interceptor squadrons of CF-lOO's which were obsolete, according to the minister, in 1957? Are they to be replaced or disbanded? What is the role of the Canadian air division in NATO? What is the attitude of the minister toward integration of the services? This is the kind of thing which surely should be discussed in a committee and a great many others, but which cannot be discussed in the committee which is visualized in this particular resolution.
If these matters are not to be discussed in a committee of this house-and the government says they are not-that in this committee all we can discuss are expenditures made between March 31, 1958 and April 1, 1959; if that is all we can discuss in this committee, when are we to discuss those questions of defence policy? Are we going to be given the opportunity in any committee, in any small committee of this house, which could summon expert witnesses; are we going to be given the opportunity to discuss these matters or in any other committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not want the hon. gentleman to name them; I want to know the nature of those experts he has in mind because this is exactly-
The leader of the Opposition has the floor.

speakerposition: Prime Minister

National Defence Committee

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the Prime Minister raising a point of order?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask you to make your ruling on this matter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

If we do not get this kind of examination of defence policy which I have mentioned, where is this examination to be given? speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The same as yours in 1952 and 1953.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I tried to point out to my hon. friend that the committee in 1951 was set up by agreement among the three parties after consultation between the prime minister of that day and the leaders of the other two parties for a purpose for which they were all agreed. As Mr. St. Laurent said at the time, it could examine matters and make reports-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: But it could not discuss policy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Even if it could not, does my hon. friend think that what was done then must be followed by this and every subsequent parliament? Was everything which the Liberal government did in 22 years so correct that this government, which was going to change everything, does not dare depart from it?
We have not apparently got our committee under this resolution. What then, can take the place of this kind of examination? Perhaps an occasional, casual reply by the minister or Prime Minister to a question-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: My replies are never casual; they are well thought out.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I acknowledge the minister's courtesy in replying to the best of his ability to every question that is asked of him in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: And very competently, too.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have no quarrel on that score. Surely, the minister himself will agree that that does not take the place of an examination of defence policy by a committee.
Mr. Pallet!: What are you supposed to do over there as Leader of the Opposition?
Keep quiet.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Or is this kind of discussion in committee, where we get to the root of these matters to be replaced by a long statement by the minister when his estimates are introduced, followed by statements from this side. We have not even had a debate on defence; we have not yet had a white paper on defence.
What is happening in other countries which are not more concerned with defence policy and defence questions than we are? What is going on in the United Kingdom in its facing up to this problem of defence? They have not been meeting as long as we have, but they have had 12J hours of discussion on defence in the month of March, based on a white paper they had been given on defence policy. What is going on in Washington? We cannot, of course, follow the procedure of congress because the parliamentary system is not the same as the congressional system. There are, however, congressional committees examining defence policy from its very foundations every day of the week. We get most of our information on continental defence, about changes in defence concept and strategy, from the reports of these committees and not through anything we get from this government in Canada. In this parliament, in this government, all we have is a fog of silence penetrated occasionally by a ministerial platitude.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in order to do our best to convert this resolution into one which will make possible the establishment of the kind of committee which will perform the functions which I have outlined and which I believe very strongly would be in the best interests of government, parliament and the country, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer):
That the motion be amended by the deletion of the words "as reported in public accounts", and by the insertion of the phrase "and the effectiveness of our defence system for the security of Canada".

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Have hon. members copies of this proposal?
No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps I should read it for their information, not by way of putting it, because before doing so I should like some assistance in determining whether the amendment, is sufficiently relevant.
As read by the Leader of the Opposition it was that the motion be amended by the deletion of the words "as reported in public accounts" in the third line of the resolution as I have it, and by the insertion of the phrase "and the effectiveness of our defence system for the security of Canada".
Mr. Pallet!: Would you read that again, please, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As proposed it would strike out the words "as reported in public accounts", and then the second proposed change after the words "the government may be effected therein", to insert the words "and the effectiveness of our defence system for the security of Canada". It would, therefore, read:
-and in particular what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of policy decided by the government may be effected therein, and the effectiveness of our defence system for the security of Canada-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I apologize, particularly to the Prime Minister and to the leader of the C.C.F. party, and to other members for not having additional copies to circulate. When I got to my amendment I thought I had five copies but I found there was only one. I do apologize.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: That happens.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I say that I have no doubt that the first proposed amendment would be relevant, that is, "as reported in public accounts". It seems to me that is within the ambit of the resolution as it is stated in the notice.
My difficulty is with the other part of the proposed resolution which adds very substantially to the terms of reference. The terms of reference now are to examine the accounts and to report. This would add explicitly the right to report on the effectiveness of our defence system for the security of Canada which, in general terms, is an authorization to consider defence policy. I think, having regard to what the Leader of the Opposition stated during the debate, that that what he has in mind is broadening the scope of the reference from one of a reference into accounts and expenditures made and a report thereon having regard to economies which might be made and so on, into a reference on the substance of defence policy and a report on that.

I would say, that would be out of line with precedents which I shall be glad to put before the house for its consideration, and I note particularly citations 291 and 293 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. An amendment to a resolution which introduces something new and different in kind into the terms of reference which the motion sets up for the committee goes too far and would require notice of motion itself before it could appear on the order paper. But before finally disposing of the matter I should be glad to hear one or two hon. members who might give some assistance on the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Your Honour made reference to citations 291 and 293. Perhaps you intended citation 203 at page 171 of Beauchesne's fourth edition which reads as follows:
203. (1) It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed.
It goes on to say this:
The law on the relevancy of amendments is that if they are on the same subject matter with the original motion, they are admissible, but not when foreign thereto.
As you pointed out, Mr. Speaker, the original motion is to investigate the expenditure of public money for national defence and there is nothing about the suggestion raised in the amendment about the effectiveness of our defence system for the security of Canada, which is an entirely different proposition. Subsection 3 of citation 203 reads as follows:
(3) An amendment setting forth a proposition dealing with a matter which is foreign to the proposition involved in the main motion is not relevant and cannot be moved.

If I may speak on this point of order, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that I believe the amendment proposed by the leader of the official opposition makes the resolution in order because, as I look at it, the resolution is not only an insult to the public accounts committee but contains nothing that is not already open to our public accounts committee and therefore is unacceptable as it appears on the order paper. I feel that the supplying of an assignment other than that regularly assigned to the public accounts committee makes out of order the government resolution as it appears on the order paper at the present time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
May I say a word on that point which has occurred to me? This resolution in its present form refers to the committee on public accounts certain public accounts dealing with defence. But only yesterday we passed a resolution referring these same public accounts to the committee on public accounts. It therefore seems to me that alteration of the resolution in this way would

National Defence Committee bring it into order rather than out of order. How can this parliament refer to two separate committees of this house the same public accounts, with orders to those committees to report back?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
May I refer Your Honour to citation 203 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, subsection 5, which reads as follows:
(5) An amendment was ruled out because It raised a new question which could only be considered on a distinct motion after notice.
Certainly the motion before us is one with regard to expenditures. Policy is a new question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think this point has been considered from time to time and I believe is reasonably well settled and explained by Beauchesne in citation 291. I begin quoting from the second paragraph:
When the house is considering a motion, of which notice has been given, for the appointment of a select committee-
That is substantially what we are doing.
-a member cannot move in amendment that the committee be given wider powers than those which were set down in the notice. On the 13th March 1938, a minister moved that a special committee be appointed to study the question of redistribution of electoral districts and to enquire into the methods whereby the source of campaign funds may be traceable. Two amendments were moved:-
And they were ruled out of order. I do not need to go into the details of the cases because I have already stated the principle. The amendments were ruled out of order
-on the ground that they raised new questions not contemplated in the notice of motion and proposed to extend the committee's powers far beyond those set down in the notice, and also that the necessity of giving notice will be nullified if such notice is not used as a guidance for the decision of the house.
Then citation 293, reading from the second sentence in that paragraph:
It is against all parliamentary usage to refer questions of policy to a fact finding committee. I find that the great Speaker Denison decided in 1877, and his decision still holds good, that "it is not competent, without notice to add a distinct question to a motion or to combine in one two distinct propositions."
On the principle that an amendment must not introduce new and different subjects to be referred to the committee, I must find that the second part of this amendment goes beyond what would be acceptable. If I might paraphrase it, in its effect it would authorize the committee to report from time to time on the effectiveness of our defence system for the security of Canada. It makes a very different reference to the committee from the one that is proposed by the government. I therefore rule that the amendment is not in order.

National Defence Committee have any such knowledge. Indeed we have been told by the Minister of National Defence that it is the intention of the government to have the leader of the house refer the estimates to this committee after we have got through the motion to go into supply. I have already heard comments from some that they do not believe it, but I will take the word of the Minister of National Defence that the estimates will be referred. Then at least we will be more up to date. We can then deal with the intended expenditures of the government.
1 do not know how you can discuss the intended expenditures of the government through the medium of estimates without discussing policy, because you would have to know what the money is being spent on and whether it should be spent. That means policy, and must mean policy. If you do not do that, then what is the use of referring the estimates at all?
As has been pointed out by the Leader of the Opposition, there is no question that every committee I, at least, have ever sat on does discuss policy as related to the matters before it. It does make recommendations on policy understandings which it gets from the various ministers, and makes decisions on those understandings. I presume that procedure will be followed when this committee is established.
I want to say that as this resolution stands before us at present it is no answer to the questions in the minds of the people and in the minds of many members in the House of Commons. It will not be able to function in a manner which will give information or a clear understanding on defence policies and where our money is going, whether it is going down the drain or whether it is serving any useful purpose. As the resolution stands now it will not give any indication as to what is in the minds of the government as to defence policy and their understanding of the rapidly changing picture in the realm of both offence and defence in international spheres. I have no hesitation in saying-and I think I speak as far as this party is concerned-that this resolution at the present time is useless. It would be a waste of time of hon. members. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: The point of order will not be settled on the issue of whether the Minister of Justice always observed the rules.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: I wonder if Your Honour would permit me just a word.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: If the hon. member would like to discuss this point of order I should like to hear him, because questions in this house for some years have very frequently taken the exact form of that asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I have had my doubts about carrying it to the degree hon. members do. Before hearing the hon. member I express the preliminary view that to found a question by referring to a statement in the press is permissible only to lay a factual foundation on which to ask a question which seeks information and not to ask a question which in effect proposes an argument based on statements in the press.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I intended, of course, no offence whatever to the Minister of Justice. I was simply seeking to use an illustration of what was the custom, and I am sure Your Honour would be the first to recognize that a very large part of the practice in all British political institutions, including this House of Commons, is based on custom and usage and not on a strict, literal interpretation of the rules, which would make almost all debates impossible.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: But not on the abuse of custom and usage.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext:
If the Minister of Justice would like to reply to me when I am finished I would be delighted to hear him. I am not defending the indiscriminate use of long extracts from the press, but it is often the easiest and simplest way to get from a minister an opinion on a matter, or a statement on a matter of fact, which has to do with the business of this house.
I must say, speaking personally, that I am not much addicted to this kind of question but I can see that it is often a great saving of the time of the house, and it does seem to me that when statements are made outside the house having directly to do with the conduct of the government, which is responsible to this house, this then is a device on which

Inquiries of the Ministry there should not be too strict an interpretation of the literal wording of the rules, in view of the long custom of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext:
I think something further
should be said on this matter. It is quite true that the rules do require an intelligent and flexible application if there is to be freedom of debate, and debate germane to the issues before the house; but an intelligent application of the rules also carries with it, as I see it, the avoidance of the abuse of custom and precedent. One of the important purposes of the rules of this house, as I apprehend them- and I believe I state it correctly-is to see that debate is carried on here between members of this House of Commons and not between members of the house and persons outside the house. Therefore the rule against reading reports of statements made by others and then asking whether ministers agree with them is to ensure that abuse will not take place, that the debate will not take the form of a minister or member of the house being drawn into a controversy with somebody outside, when that debate or controversy should take place in the house.
It is tempting, I know, to members to try to draw ministers into controversy with people outside the house, and to get the controversy going on those grounds. Nothing would be more attractive to the opposition than if they could, for instance, get a controversy going between the Minister of Justice and the president of the exchequer court; and that was, whether intentional or not, certainly the effect of the question asked. That would be a very improper thing, and it was to avoid that very sort of situation and to keep the debate within the house, that the salutary rule and precedent have grown up which say that questions may not be asked which take the form of the reading of statements made by somebody outside the house and asking ministers whether they have any comment to make thereon.
Whether or not the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate desires, not to use that custom but to abuse any flexibility that has been given in the application of that rule, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this particular instance is indeed an illustration of the way in which any flexibility that has been allowed is beginning to be abused. It was because I objected to the abuse of the flexibility that I raised the point of order with regard to this particular question.
I come back to what seems to me to be a very simple proposition. If I were to comply with the hon. gentleman's request for a comment I would very probably be drawn into controversy with the president of the

Exchequer court instead of with the member for Vancouver East, and that is a situation into which I refuse to be drawn, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to say something in view of the long lecture we have just received from the Minister of Justice; indeed, not only a lecture directed against the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who, in his desire to see the rules of this house observed-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT

speechtext: I was seeking to do that very thing, but as soon as I make the effort hon. gentlemen opposite with their big majority make it impossible for me to do so.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
