subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: The hon. member is proceeding in the wrong direction. What he has the floor for is to discuss the point of order and not the arrogance of some other member of the house.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, may I say with great respect that if the Minister of Justice had been reminded that he has certain responsibilities in this house it would not have been necessary for me to use what I think in the circumstances was a very apt description of the speech made by the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: We know you are back, Paul.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice has said that the purpose of questions at this particular point in our proceedings is to encourage the eliciting of information by a member of the house from a minister. I would say if that is not to be the interpretation, then parliament would be taking a step that would result in a serious abridgement of its functions and its opportunities. Pursuant to our custom, surely it is open to any member of the house on the orders of the day to ask a member of the government for comment with respect to something that may have been said outside the house on matters of public interest with regard to the operations of the government of Canada. If we are to take the position which the Minister of Justice has asserted, then there will be an abridgement of free speech in this parliament such as in my experience has never been suggested before.
Let us say that the president of the institute of international affairs made a comment with regard to foreign policy. Would it not be proper for any member of the house to rise and ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs for his comment one way or the other?

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice, indicating the absurdity of the position he has taken in this argument, now says that he must not be drawn into an argument between the president of the exchequer court and himself as a member of the executive. Since when must there be acceptance of that enunciation of that position? Surely if the president of the exchequer court, in a capacity other than his judicial capacity makes an observation of public concern and interest, it is proper for a member of the house to ask for the opinion of the Minister of Justice. The latter need not, under the traditions of the house, give an answer, but certainly a member is not to be precluded from putting the question.
Nor would a member be precluded from asking the Minister of Justice to comment on a statement of national interest made by the president of the exchequer court in his judicial capacity. Prime ministers and home secretaries in the parliament of the United Kingdom have not hesitated to comment on statements of Her Majesty's judges in matters of public concern. Therefore if we were to follow the hastily considered argument of the Minister of Justice we would be destroying one of the important instruments of free discussion in this house; and I would urge Your Honour, if you are at all tempted to
Inquiries of the Ministry accept the weak argument put forward by the Minister of Justice, that it might be better for Your Honour, in view of the importance of this matter, to give it further consideration later this day or on some other day.
In my opinion it would be a serious abridgement of our rights if we were to be denied the opportunity which the minister is now seeking to deny us. I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that day by day during the course of this session we have had increasing evidence of the desire of the administration to curb free debate in this house.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: The hon. member is now going beyond discussion of the point of order. If the hon. member is finished, I shall be glad to deal with the point.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext:
May I
respectfully refer you, Mr. Speaker, to Beau-chesne's fourth edition, citation 178 at page 152, as authority for the proposition that attention may only be drawn to articles in newspapers if the hon. member drawing attention to the article is prepared to vouch for the accuracy of the statement in the newspaper. I doubt very much whether this house is prepared to accept the opinion of the hon. member as to the accuracy of this statement. I humbly submit that in the circumstances no exception should be made in this instance in contravention of the rules.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: Was it citation 178 to which the hon. member mentioned?

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext:
I just want to say a few words on the point of order. On many occasions, Mr. Speaker, it has been pointed out by yourself that procedure in this house is governed by standing orders of the house, by precedent and by custom. As you will recall, you have often pointed out that custom supercedes precedent.
I draw the attention of Your Honour to this fact, which is borne out not only by your own long experience here but may I say by my own experience in the seven years I have been in this house. In the questioning on the orders of the day I would say, as an approximation, that over 50 per cent of all questions are based on newspaper reports and quotations, and that very rarely are they ruled out on that basis. In this present session in particular I would say that almost 75 per cent of the questions have been preceded by the words "Has the minister any comment to make or any view to express"; then there is direct reference

Inquiries of the Ministry to something in the Globe and Mail or Gazette or some other newspaper.
On the basis of that situation I am asking whether this is not in order. I should like to add, if I may, to the Minister of Justice that I was particularly careful not to make any reference to Mr. Thorson as president of the exchequer court, because he was speaking not as such but as the president of the international commission of jurists.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: May I have the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to make one further comment?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: Has the minister something further to add?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext:
Yes, I have this comment to add. We are referred to custom and precedent, and then it is suggested that it has become established custom and precedent for questions to be asked based upon reports in newspapers. The comment I would make there is that it is true that this has been a growing tendency, during this session particularly and perhaps during last session. But my point now is this. If we do not raise the question now, if it goes without observation and without objection, it will become an established custom. The point of order I raised was that it is not permitted under our rule. It is true that on occasion, in order to apply the rule flexibly, it has been permitted; but it is not permitted by the rule, and I am simply seeking the application of the rule.
It is because I am concerned that if the custom is allowed to grow unchecked it will then be taken as a rule that I am raising the matter now. The rule is clear. Beau-chesne's fourth edition is the latest authoritative statement. It was published in 1958; it is not an old or outdated publication. May I just refer Your Honour to two passages. The first is found at page 148, citation 171, which states:
A question oral or written must not:
- (z) refer to speeches made outside the house;
The second citation is 177, which states:
177. Reading telegrams, letters or extracts from newspapers as an opening to a question when the orders of the day are called is an abuse of the rules of the house.
Hence I think the situation is quite clear.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: Bead the whole paragraph (z).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext:
I will read the next sentence, which is as follows:
It is not good parliamentary practice to communicate written allegations to the house and then to ask ministers either to confirm or deny them.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: I was referring to paragraph (z).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: The hon. member can read the citation he wishes to read.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext: If the minister does not want to read it, we will do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext:
It is clear that the rule there is that the question must be the member's own question. That is the basic principle. It is true that sometimes, in order to give a member an opportunity to make his question clear, reference to newspapers reporting statements made outside the house is permitted. But my recollection is perfectly clear also that Speakers have always been properly concerned to avoid abuse of this flexibility and to avoid a situation where a member, instead of making a question his own- instead of asking his own question-uses a statement reported to be made in a newspaper and then asks a minister to comment on it. The basic rule of debate is that speeches must be the speeches of the member himself, and that questions must be the questions of the member himself.
Contrary to what the hon. member for Essex East has said, I have not taken the position directly or by implication that such matters as are raised here cannot be raised. Certainly the Minister of Justice can be asked whether his view on a certain proposal is this way or that way. However, my point is that no minister should be asked by a member whether he agrees with a statement on a matter of government policy which is made by someone else and for which the member does not take responsibility. The question should be a question raised by the member of parliament, not a question raised by somebody else however eminent that other person may be. That is my purpose in raising the matter this morning.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT
speechtext:
I have taken an undue amount of the time of the house to hear the views of hon. members, as I think this is an important matter. As was suggested, I should like to give some more reflective thought to it and try to express what is contained in the citations to which I have been referred and the practice of the house in perhaps more considered terms. Undoubtedly it has been decided on many occasions, for example, as stated in Beauchesne's fourth edition in citation 177:
177. Reading telegrams, letters or extracts from newspapers as an opening to a question when the orders of the day are called is an abuse of the rules of the house.
The point raised by the minister was that the question which may arise from such a reading very often can properly be asked as a request for information or a question as to the intentions of the government. But to introduce it as a request for comment on an

opinion of somebody else may not be the proper approach to seeking information which the house is entitled to obtain from the administration. Basically, this is not a time for debate or argument. It is a time in which to get information on current matters of urgent public interest.
To get back to the matter in point, I think the question asked by the hon. member is objectionable in the form in which he has presented it. Therefore, without concluding this discussion-as I say, I should like to take the matter under advisement-I suggest that in asking the Minister of Justice to express an opinion on an opinion which somebody else has expressed outside the house as reported, in a newspaper, particularly on the subject matter which he raises, is asking for an opinion on policy of the government expressed as a comment on someone's opinion outside the house; and in that form the minister is correct in objecting to this specific question.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO EXAMINE EXPENDITURES

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, March 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearkes for the appointment of a special committee to examine defence expenditures.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the most important consideration in connection with this proposed resolution is simply whether or not it will permit the task which must be accomplished. The answer to that question, in our opinion, is that it will not.
The reasoning behind the request for this special committee on the part of the leader of the Liberal party was that in his opinion, and in the opinion of all hon. members on this side of the house, the change in the situation in the last few years has been so dramatic and so marked that only by a full and frank discussion of all the information available can this house and the Canadian people be satisfied with respect to the direction of defence matters.
My hon. leader felt that some of the money being spent on defence is not being well spent, and his view is shared by many Canadians. This concern is not so much for those small items of waste and extravagance about which hon. members opposite talked so much when they were on this side of the house, and which there is no reason to believe are any less evident at the present time than they were then, but rather with respect to big items of expenditure which are within the framework of the government's present policy. Are these the correct expenditures for Canada to be making, and can the government gives us any information not previously disclosed to justify its position?
Defence problems today are very complex, and this cannot be denied. The change since 1951 has been fundamental, and from the period of 1957, when the first sputnik was fired, the rapidity with which new inventions and new weapons have been disclosed is almost beyond our comprehension. The latest Soviet and United States shots of intercontinental ballistic missiles over ranges of thousands of miles, with an accuracy within a radius of one and a half or two miles, is of so startling a character that they cannot longer be ignored by thinking Canadians.
Anyone in charge of Canadian defence policy at the present time has a very difficult task. No one denies that. We must take into account, at the same time, the defence policy of the western world. We are members of an alliance, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and our policies-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of
order, if the hon. member is going to discuss the defence policy either of Canada or of the western alliance, as he appears to be doing, I suggest he is out of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes. I remind the hon.
member for Trinity that I stopped the minister when he began his statement on this
National Defence
motion when he was proceeding in the same direction as the hon. member is going, and I request him to keep within the limits that have been set by our rules and observed so far.

I am happy to abide by
that decision, Mr. Speaker. Actually I am convinced that there is nothing in my notes which could be considered as relating strictly to the nature of defence policy as such. I have made reference to a bit of background information and the scope and breadth of the problem which I feel is relevant to this resolution because it is the basis for the resolution and the only reason why the committee was asked for at the outset. I shall be very careful, however, not to depart from this general framework. I have no intention of discussing defence policy at this time but will do so on a later occasion.
As I say our policies have to be complementary to those of our allies and particularly to those of our United States neighbour, because unless they are-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the point of order, the hon. member has just said that he proposes to do what the minister was prevented from doing last night. The minister's point was that since the committee was discussing expenditures in line with the government's policy, he would outline the policy. It was a decision of Your Honour on the advice of hon. members opposite that this should not be done. I do not believe it would be correct for the hon. member now to do exactly the same thing, based on the same argument.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: As I understood the last remarks of the hon. member who has the floor, he was proceeding to say what our policy had to be in these days, and it seems to me that in doing so he is going beyond the scope of the debate.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I do not share the view expressed by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Chambers). I do not believe I have transgressed, but if you feel that I do from this point on I am sure you will draw it to my attention.
Anyone who has followed the debate in Washington realizes the tremendous difference of opinion which exists in the world at the present time in respect to these matters. This cannot be denied. There is a tremendous variation of opinion both in this country and throughout the western world. Indeed, the Prime Minister on January 20, when speaking in this house, referred to General Maxwell

National Defence
Taylor's book. This, I feel, is required reading for all who are interested in the subject.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I think he should revise his thinking about what is relevant. The resolution is one to set up a committee to consider the expenditures of the Department of National Defence. It is relevant to the debate to indicate the desirability of setting up that committee and to discuss in general terms that principle. The principle is whether a committee should be set up to consider expenditures. The principle is not that of whether the committee should be set up to consider the policy of Canada with respect to national defence.
It seems to me the hon. member is attempting to discuss a matter beyond the scope of this resolution. I have already allowed the Leader of the Opposition, in his remarks yesterday, to say that he felt the resolution should include that subject, defence policy, but in allowing that latitude it does not permit a discussion of what policies should be referred to the committee and why they should be referred, which is what the hon. member is basically referring to.

Surely, Mr. Speaker, the corollary of an inadequate resolution is an adequate one. The whole purpose of asking for this committee to be set up was to discuss defence policy in its fullest and most comprehensive form. That is what the Leader of the Opposition asked for, that is what we thought we were getting, and that is what we want. Anything else is, in our opinion, completely inadequate. Surely some reference to what we feel should be discussed in this committee and what we feel is relevant, is appropriate to the subject under discussion, and relates to the reasons why we feel the present resolution is completely inadequate.
It was because of this dependence and interdependence, the differences of opinion and the increasing complexity of defence that we felt a more comprehensive and general discussion should take place. When the Prime Minister mentioned that this committee would be set up, as reported at page 143 of Hansard of January 20, 1960 he said:
But in the light of all the circumstances, it will review the expenditures to the end that the ability, the training and the capacity of members in every part of the house may be used for the purpose of examining this most important problem.
Those were the Prime Minister's words. That is what we expected we were going to get when the Prime Minister told us he would accept our suggestion. It sounded like a genuine desire to set up a committee to work out for this country a bipartisan defence

policy. It was so interpreted by us and indeed it was so interpreted by many people in the country, including much of the press; because there were reports at the time to the effect that here at last was an opportunity being presented to parliament and to the Canadian people to come to grips with this important problem and to work it out in such a way that the Canadian people would know whether or not they were getting value for the money being spent, whether or not they were getting protection, or indeed whether or not any protection is possible in this day.
It was this type of full debate that we on this side of the house asked for and to which we felt we were entitled, one where all the facts could be presented. We feel it is not good enough to have the facts simply up to April, 1959. This house has not been given any body of facts on the subject of defence great enough on which to base intelligent judgment, probably less than in any other democratic parliament in the world.
We feel that although there are some places where perhaps too much information is given, certainly in this country we are being given much too litle. We interpreted the Prime Minister's concurrence to mean that the facts would be given and that the policies would be discussed in full, not just the expenditures for the fiscal period April, 1958 to April, 1959, as included in the public accounts and as set out in the resolution before us.
A wide discussion would not be an abdication of the government's responsibility. It is still part of the government's responsibility to get the widest possible discussion to confirm its own collective mind in respect to its policies. That is part of the business of policy making. That is how decisions are arrived at.
We in the official opposition have been criticized in the press and in the country because our criticisms of the defence policy of Canada were too much directed to single articles of military hardware, and in some respects that is a valid criticism of us. But how can we discuss the greater problems of the Canadian defence policy in the framework of NATO defence policy unless we have greater access to the facts, a fuller and more complete disclosure of the various background material available to the government and to the Minister of National Defence?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member accept a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: When the hon. member refers to having access to a greater volume of material, I presume of course he refers to classified material?

Not necessarily, Mr. Speaker. I know from experience that the information we are getting is a very small proportion of the non-classified material. I think there is some material which is classified which could be made available to hon. members at no security risk whatever. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, if you will allow me this much indulgence, that recently a dispatch from Washington surprised us when we learned that a bow and arrow had been classified as top secret. There are quite a few secrets in the defence department which are not really secrets at all. They are secrets only to the Canadian people. They are certainly not secrets to the Russians. They are not secrets to the Americans, who have a very frank and full disclosure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Is he not aware that Canada threw out its last bow and arrow shortly after he left the department?
I am aware-
They threw out the Arrow.
I am aware that they scrapped their best Arrow and I am sure they now have second thoughts, particularly since the government are being requested to replace it with inferior weapons from elsewhere.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: How do you know?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Because it does not work.

Mr. Speaker, we do not get the facts from our own government, but we do manage to get some from other, more friendly governments. I can assure you we are very grateful that some of those other sources are available to us. We are, as a consequence, very disappointed to read this motion. We could scarcely believe our eyes when it was printed in Votes and Proceedings, a motion with precisely the same scope and breadth as if it were setting up the public accounts committee, or referring this matter to the public accounts committee. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, it is an insult to the public accounts committee, as was stated last night, because it is a duplication; it allows no more freedom of latitude than would be permitted to the public accounts committee except, of course, that probably there will
National Defence
be a supporter of the government as chairman of this particular committee, which would not be so in the public accounts committee.
This particular resolution, Mr. Speaker, is also not so broad as would be a reference of the current estimates to the estimates committee. This is, I say, most disturbing because we were clearly under the impression, the Canadian people were clearly under the impression, that something more was being given, something more was being proposed; not something less, not something which was already available to us. All this will do is permit us to examine the expenditures for the period April, 1958 to April, 1959, and to recommend suggestions as to economies that can be effected within the framework of the government policy existing at that time. These are retroactive savings in respect of money already spent. This is an academic point, really, at this stage, and I am sure is of small comfort to this house and to the Canadian people. What is the government afraid of?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Nothing.

Nothing; the government has nothing to fear but fear itself. It should welcome a full discussion. The Prime Minister keeps referring back to 1951. The world is not the same as it was in 1951; things have changed. Perhaps the government wishes it could turn back the clock, but it cannot. Consideration of today's problems in terms of 1951 is futile. In 1951 some military experts were saying they would not live to see the day when an intercontinental ballistic missile would be operational. To talk today in terms of 1951 only underscores the government's head in the sand attitude toward defence matters.
As a matter of fact, a basic difference between Conservatives and Liberals is apparent. The Conservatives are looking back to 1951 and using the precedents of that day as appropriate to this day, while the Liberals are looking forward, at least to 1965, to try to find out what policies would be suitable in the middle of the 1960's, as far as can be projected at the present time. Some people in this house would call that planning; others would call it vision, and still others would call it good management.
I call it just so many words.

In 1951 the United States had not yet exploded its first megaton bomb and the Russians did not do so until 1953, and the situation in the 1951-1953 era was still understandable in terms of world war II conventional knowledge and understanding. It is not so today. The situation has changed

National Defence
to such an extent that developments in the meantime, and those going on at the present time, tax the imagination of even those people who follow the matter closely and who have some technical background with which to interpret it.
It is futile to consider expenditures from April, 1958 to April, 1959 to the exclusion of those more recent developments and the projection of future developments. Why, then, will the government not permit a broader discussion? It will have a majority on the committee. Its followers will undoubtedly dominate the committee. The committee will not report or make suggestions which are not compatible with the beliefs or have not the support of the government majority on that committee, and even if it should make recommendations which the government is not inclined to implement, the government does not have to accept this advice. The government is not bound by this advice; the government can take it or leave it, but at least it would have the benefit of the advice and consideration of members on all sides of this house.
Why should the minister not answer policy matters in committee? He has to do so in this house when there is a debate on national defence matters; he has to do so in committee of the whole house when his estimates are before us. Why is it any different with respect to answering policy matters before a special select committee? As a matter of fact the atmosphere there is more conducive to a non-partisan discussion; the mere physical appointments are more conducive to intelligent, easy study of very important and far-reaching problems. In addition, there the minister can allow his officials, if he wishes to do so, to make direct answers to questions. This speeds up the proceedings and gives members the benefit of a greater amount of technical and other advice. There are many advantages in having a full and complete discussion in committee, and I cannot understand why the minister and the government are afraid to allow this type of discussion.
When in opposition many of the present members of the government asked for just this kind of committee. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes), the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), and others all asked for this same kind of comprehensive discussion which we are now asking for. They are all on record, Mr. Speaker.
I will not take the trouble to read their remarks into the record, but they are in the books and available to anyone who wishes to read them. I am sure at the moment the

ministers are perhaps trying to forget them, but if they felt strongly-and we must assume they did; they would not have spoken if they were not speaking sincerely-if they felt that a full and complete discussion of defence matters was appropriate at that time when defence matters were much less complicated than they are today, why in the name of logic and consistency would they feel differently now? Why would they not feel the same now? Why would they not welcome and encourage this type of full and free discussion that the Leader of the Opposition and the Liberal party have been asking for?
Last night the government tried to make the point that committees should not discuss policy. The Leader of the Opposition cited a case-he cited more than one case, as a matter of fact-where policy has been discussed, such as the committee on external affairs. There are other examples.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit another question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. member give us an example in the last few years when a committee on external affairs recommended on policy matters to the government?

Mr. Speaker, I have no knowledge offhand of whether it has made recommendations, but we are talking about discussion. We do not feel that the committee necessarily has to tell the government what to do; but the government, after listening, can make up its own mind and act on its own responsibility, which is its constitutional duty. All we are asking for is an opportunity to have the discussion so the government will be able to benefit from it. Will the hon. member who has interjected deny that there has been discussion of policy in the committee on external affairs?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister was complaining this morning that we had not brought up certain policy questions.

As the Leader of the Opposition has just said, the minister was complaining this morning because policy matters had not been brought up. There are other examples. Here is one. On today's order paper we have item No. 8, which reads as follows:
The following proposed motion: (1) That a select committee be appointed to consider the policy, operations and expenditures of the national research council, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon.
It is to be appointed to consider policy, not to consider past expenditures which are of more or less academic interest. There are

18, I860
other examples. Here is one. In the Journals of the House of Commons for 1959 we find the following at page 359:
Mrs. Fairclough, seconded by Mr. Nowlan, moved, -That a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons be appointed to examine and consider the Indian Act, chapter 149,	R.S.C., 1952, and
amendments thereto, and to suggest such amendments as they may deem advisable, with authority to investigate and report upon Indian administration in general and, in particular, on the social and economic status of the Indians.
Here is an example of a government invitation to a committee, in this case of both houses, to consider policy, to examine into questions of substance and to make recommendations in respect thereof.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not dealing with classified material.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the committee would not make recommendations which disclosed classified material. Any classified material which the government felt it could produce could be produced in camera, as is done when the subcommittee of congress on appropriations is holding its hearings. We do not wish to make public any material which would jeopardize our security, but I can assure the hon. member that a great amount of the classified material in the defence department could be made available to the Canadian public without any detriment whatsoever to national security. As a matter of fact the Canadian people would have a better idea of what is going on if that did happen, and I for one think much of it could be made public, and that it would be in the public interest to do so.
I have given examples of committees that have been invited and allowed to discuss policy matters, and there are other examples. It is obvious that a committee can, that committees have and that committees will discuss policy when it is expedient or convenient for the government of the day to allow them so to do.
The resolution in its present form is an affront to parliament. Even more important, it is an affront to the Canadian people. Many Canadians are confused and bewildered by the sparse and conflicting information available, and surely a discussion which would help to clarify the situation is indeed in order. Surely the question of national survival and the expenditure of $1.6 billion of the taxpayers' money is of such overwhelming importance that those of us who have been elected to hold the public trust must do everything possible to satisfy ourselves and the public in this regard.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, we implore the government to change the resolution. We
National Defence
implore the government even at this late stage to amend the resolution on its own initiative and make it the kind of resolution which will permit the type of committee that hon. members opposite sought when they were on this side of the house, and which is so much more appropriate and urgent at the present time than it was then.
We hope they will do this. We urge them to do it in the name of the Canadian people whose trust we hold. If the government will not do so then the official opposition, which believes that the resolution in its present form, permitting as it does only a discussion of expenditures which took place between April, 1958 and 1959, which is completely and hopelessly inadequate, will be duty bound to vote against it.

In fact the Leader of the Opposition moved an amendment calling for just that last night. It seems to me that what in fact they are calling for is a United States type of committee.

speechtext: Nonsense.

speechtext: I know the Leader of the Opposition denied that last night-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am denying it again this morning.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: -but just today the hon. member for Trinity made comparisons with the appropriations committee of congress. We do not want to disparage the system whereby the United States arrives at their defence policy. That is their business. A great deal of their policy is dictated in committees of the House of Representatives and the Senate. That, as I say, is their system. Our system is different. We too have a system for arriving at defence policy. The system is clearly known to hon. members opposite. Responsible officers and chiefs of staff make their recommendations to the government through the Minister of National Defence. Those recommendations are then brought to parliament and parliament decides policy. It either approves or disapproves-
That is a strange doctrine.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
-the policies that are put forward by the government. It does this on a number of occasions, particularly at the time the estimates of the department are brought forward. This has been our practice since parliament has sat. It is the practice in the parliament of Great Britain, from

National Defence
which we take so many of our traditions. What the opposition has in fact suggested is a change in the entire system of arriving at policy.
That is not so at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The Leader of the Opposition suggested that experts should be called before the committee to testify on policy. He did not say at that time what experts he wanted but he said he did not want, and I am perfectly delighted to agree with him, serving officers called before the committee. Perhaps the expert he had in mind was the hon. member for Trinity.
He is a very good one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: As a matter of fact, I do not disagree with either the Leader of the Opposition or the hon. member for Trinity that defence policy should be discussed. We have been waiting anxiously in the house through 10 days of the throne speech debate and through two supply motions to hear the views of hon. members opposite.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You promised then to set up a committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We offered last night to institute a debate on defence policy.

On a question of privilege, the parliamentary secretary has just said that they waited with bated breath through the throne speech. I made a speech on defence in that debate, and the Minister of National Defence did not when he had the opportunity to do so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He did not even speak in the throne speech debate.
The Leader of the Opposition also spoke.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I will have to plead guilty, because the splash made by the speech of my hon. friend was not loud enough for me to hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Not one speech was made on that side.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Certainly we were advised through the press before the house met in January that the opposition had tremendous criticisms to make of our defence policy, and had valuable ideas to put forward. This, of course, is a very serious matter. It is a matter concerning which everybody who has a point of view should make that point of view known. But so far, as I say, I am afraid that the policy changes the opposition would like to have made have not seen the light of day. Perhaps they cannot stand the light of day.

Last night, when the Minister of National Defence announced that he had secured the agreement of the house leader to have the current estimates of the department referred to this committee when they come up for consideration, this announcement caused a great deal of alarm and despondency, and I personally was very much surprised.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It cannot be done under the rules.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: There was no obligation on the part of the government to disclose that this would be done. However, the government thought it would be fair to tell the house, and particularly the opposition, that in future the deliberations of this committee would be widened so they would have before them not merely the public accounts that are mentioned in this resolution but would also have the expenditures proposed for the coming year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why did you vote down the amendment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: May I point out that this would be a broader term of reference than that of any defence committee that was set up when my hon. friends were sitting on this side of the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why did you vote down the amendment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I should like to quote from the prime minister of that day. In 1951 Mr. St. Laurent, as reported at page 971 of Hansard of that year, had this to say. I do not need to go into the terms of reference of that committee. As the Leader of the Opposition said last night, they are greatly similar.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It was broader than this one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. St. Laurent said this:
I do not believe there will be any generosity of interpretation of the terms of reference required because they are very specific.
I could quote at some length, but time after time in that address the prime minister of that day mentioned things which the committee could not talk about. They could not talk about allowances to widows and dependants. They could not talk about policy. They would not have serving officers before them, and so on. In fact it was a speech of restriction.
The resolution we have before us to set up the committee will enable hon. members opposite to examine the expenditures which have been made by the Department of National Defence, and when the estimates are referred to it that will enable the committee

to examine the current and proposed expenditures on national defence. When the estimates come back before the house or, if hon. members opposite so desire, during debate on a supply motion, Canada's policy on national defence can be debated exhaustively where it should be debated, namely in the House of Commons where it always has been debated.
I think it is also important to notice what happened during a good deal of the period to which the hon. member for Trinity was referring, namely 1953 until the present. He picks out 1953 as a particularly important date, because it was then that the Soviet union divulged the fact that it had atomic weapons. During the period from 1953 to 1957 there was no committee on defence of any sort, notwithstanding the continual requests from the opposition of the day that there should be an examination in the light of the new developments.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Now you have a chance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
There was no committee on expenditures. There was no committee of any sort. Already since 1958 we have referred the 1958 estimates of the Department of National Defence to the estimates committee, where a thorough investigation was made. But in all that period during which the whole fundamental change in defence strategy took place, as the hon. member has pointed out, no committee was permitted even though in 1951, when the committee of that day was set up, the then prime minister said "I think now this should be a continuing committee."
When hon. members opposite suggest that this government denies information to members, that this government stifles discussion, may I say that the opposite is the truth. Since this government came into power there has been more examination of the workings of government, through the committee system, than happened during the whole period when hon. members opposite were in office. The committee system had almost fallen into disuse, in that many special committees which were indicated were not set up, and that references of such things as estimates, public accounts and so on to committees were few and far between.
I was going to mention the fact that last night the Leader of the Opposition suggested that the committee on external affairs make recommendations on policy. That matter was raised this morning, and I think it has been established that such is not the case. There are excellent debates on external affairs policy. There was one in this house not long ago. The Leader of the Opposition gave his views. No doubt in due time, when
National Defence
they have had a chance to formulate some ideas on this subject, hon. members opposite will speak in the House of Commons and give their ideas on defence policy. But the place to do that is in the House of Commons. We in this country believe that, as part of our constitutional system, government policy should be established by the government and should be brought before parliament, where the government takes responsibility before parliament and the people for that policy. It is not our intention to slough off this responsibility on any committee. The responsibility for policy lies with the government and parliament. That is where it should be and where it should remain.
You have not accepted your responsibility. That is the reason we are so greatly concerned. You have no policy at the present time. We expected to hear it earlier than this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: We have an interruption from the other side of the house, and I absolve the Liberal party. I am not permitted at this time to explain exactly the changes and the improvements made and the general housecleaning that had to be done and was done by this government when it came into power, changing the defence policy from what it was in those days.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am a little bit worried about you.

The hon. gentleman talks about the housecleaning that had to be done. Does the hon. gentleman recall that the present Minister of National Defence, shortly after he took office, said that he found everything in excellent order?
They got the horses off the payroll before then.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Thank you very much. Everything was in order from the point of view of the personnel-and the very fine personnel, I might say-who serve in Canada's armed forces. But from the point of view of administration and policy, I do not think anyone can deny the fact that great changes were necessary, in fact were overdue at that time; and they were made.
We can hardly wait to hear what they were.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is getting a little bit off the track.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Someone held the carrot in front of me, Mr. Speaker. I have little more to say. I have pointed out to the house that this committee with its present terms of

National Defence
reference, and when in due course the estimates of the department are referred to it, will have a wider field for investigation in matters of defence than any defence committee that has been set up previously in this house. This committee will examine and report on the expenditures that have been made and are proposed to be made. In the House of Commons itself policy may be discussed, and between those two procedures the whole field of national defence will be covered.
Would the hon. member permit a question? When making that statement is he referring to the present resolution or to the proposed one referred to last night?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I thought I made it clear that I referred to both.

Under the circumstances,
would you move the amendment today to broaden the resolution to cover both references?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Unfortunately the rules do not permit it.
We will give unanimous consent.

Mr. Speaker, I want to reiterate our contention that this resolution ought not to be supported, and in doing so give my reasons so there will be no misrepresentation when the members of our group rise in their places to cast their votes against this resolution.
We have for years called for the establishment of a committee to inquire into the policies of the government in relation to national defence. We feel that the government in a country such as ours, and governments in other democratic parts of the world, in order to provide really effective defence must have a broad understanding with its taxpayers with regard to defence policy, as broadly spread among the people as possible. We are weakening our defence if we fail to take the public into our confidence to the greatest possible extent consistent with the security needs of the nation.
We are therefore extremely disappointed at the limitations contained within this resolution, and I had hoped that after the debate yesterday evening the government would not have insisted upon continuing this debate today. Rather I had hoped that the government would take this matter under advisement and come up with another proposal.
We have been told in this house by the minister that the estimates may be referred to this committee; and we all know the minister well enough and accept his word,

as we have to accept his word. It is because of this announcement by the minister that we fail to understand why the government insists in leaving in the resolution the words "as reported in public accounts". If it is intending to refer the estimates to this committee, why does the government insist upon the retention of those words? The retention of those words certainly limits the activities of the committee which is proposed.
I had also hoped that overnight the government would have looked at another part of the resolution and given real consideration to a revision of that part. The resolution, in part, says:
-and in particular what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein-
I would like to underline what the hon. member for Vancouver East said last night, because I had hoped the government would take his remarks under advisement. I hope even now that we may be informed as to how it is possible to recommend economies on expenditures that have already been made. You cannot possibly recommend a saving of money which has already been spent, and in that respect the resolution is rather inconsistent in that any recommendation calling for economies is just impossible as long as the limitation in the earlier part of the resolution remains.
The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Defence emphasized that the place to discuss policy is in this House of Commons, and I have to agree with him. However, he also knows that one is able in a committee, which has power to call for the production of persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses, to obtain much more information than one is able to obtain in the house itself. It is for that reason that for many years we have urged that a committee be established to look into national defence policy.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand the reason for a resolution of this kind appearing on the order paper. The government is aware that this is one of our major national problems, of growing concern to a growing number of Canadian taxpayers. People in all political parties and in all walks of life are beginning to demand in a louder voice each year that there be a real examination of government defence policy. However, I am afraid that the terms of this resolution are going to be very disappointing to the Canadian people.
This resolution appears to me as a beautifully wrapped gift box containing nothing. It seems to be rather in line with the government's approach to other major national

problems, such as the unemployment question and its teeny winter works program. On major national problems with which this government is charged, it presents to the Canadian people what is in fact a beautifully wrapped gift box containing nothing.
We cannot sustain this kind of farce. We cannot help the government to mislead the Canadian people into believing that there is going to be this examination of national defence policy, which examination we feel is so vital and so urgent. Mr. Speaker, because we cannot support the government in its efforts to pull the wool over the taxpayers' eyes, we in this group intend to vote against this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in this debate, nor will I be very long in my remarks. However I, as other hon. members in the house, cannot quite see why the government is so reluctant to discuss this vital question of defence policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not reluctant at all.

Every hon. member who has
spoken has made mention of the fact that in this era of intercontinental ballistic missiles our whole system of defence has been changed. It is because it has become such a technical question that we feel that the fullest and freest discussion should be held at this time.
One of the reasons why I rise to make a few short remarks is that I found in Hansard for November 13, 1951, a statement made by the leader of the opposition of that day. I think it is quite fitting that this statement should be read into the record now. I also believe it expresses a realism which the then leader of the opposition had at that time which should now be adopted by the members of the Conservative party in their attitude toward this new era of national defence. Mr. Drew had this to say, as reported on page 961 of Hansard for November 13, 1951:
I made it clear that the reason I was discussing the defence situation and the threat abroad was that we might know how important it is that when this committee meets it be given the widest powers, such powers as have been defined by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent).
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that everyone is in agreement that the powers which should be given to the committee should be such that we can go into all the difficult angles of our national defence policy in this new era. Anything less than the powers for which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) asked would be completely unrealistic.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Did you agree with Mr. Drew then?
National Defence

I stated that I agree, and I
think everyone in this house has stated it, that what we want is to be able to discuss the government's policy on defence with all its implications.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member did not answer my question.

Further in the course of the debate there were suggestions that the opposition had not taken the opportunity of bringing the subject of national defence forward for discussion. As has already been mentioned, the hon. member for Trinity spoke on this subject during the debate on the address and so did the Leader of the Opposition, although the Minister of National Defence unfortunately did not speak. If indeed the government was anxious to have this subject debated in the house I should like to ask this question, and perhaps the minister will reply. Why was it that the government chose to bring forward the estimates of the Department of Agriculture rather than the estimates of the Department of National Defence, if it had really been the wish of the government that the house should debate defence matters without delay? It seems to me the government could have brought forward the estimates of the Department of National Defence before those of the Department of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must inform the house that if the minister speaks now he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
This rather wide-ranging debate on the setting up of this committee to investigate the expenditures of the Department of National Defence and to give such advice in connection with economies as the com-mitteee may see fit, within the policy of the government, has centred very largely on the question of the enlargement of the terms of reference of this committee. It has been suggested that the committee should discuss the policies of the government. The Leader of the Opposition, referring to this proposed committee on January 20, said:
-so that we may assist in working out a national committee on defence on the broadest possible basis.
The hon. member for Trinity also referred to a bipartisan policy which could be introduced. Now, it is a British tradition which has been accepted by Canada for many, many years that our parliamentary system is divided into a government with its supporters and an opposition. The whole point of this system is that there may be

National Defence
the expression of different opinions, that the opposition has the right to criticize government policy. Except in times of the gravest emergency, such as in time of war, it has not been the policy of Canadian governments to have a union government; it has not been the policy to accept the idea of a bipartisan policy. If we did that, discussion would be stifled in this house.
One can see that there are many urgent matters with regard to which it might be said that it would be desirable for a unified policy to be adopted; not only in the field of defence but perhaps in the field of transportation, which today presents many very difficult problems. Perhaps there should be a bipartisan policy in connection with agriculture. There has been a lot of discussion regarding agricultural policy from time to time. But that is not the policy; that is not the system under which we operate in this country. It is traditional that any government must take responsibility for policy in respect to defence matters or any other matter.
It is interesting to see that there is really no unified policy so far as hon. members of the opposition are concerned. In 1958 the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) had this to say when the estimates committee was being set up:
I was extremely pleased to hear-and as my leader was, I too am very much in accord with it- what the Prime Minister said about ministerial responsibility and the obligation of keeping the responsibility for policy in the ministry and excepting policy questions from the purview of the committee. This is the view which I took when I first appeared before the committee at its very first session at the beginning of the proceedings in 1955. I set out the position of ministerial responsibility that was then taken, and I am happy to say that there was no real dissent in the committee from that position.
That would indicate a certain variation of opinion as between hon. members opposite.
When we have set up the committee I hope the closest examination will be given to these expenditures, not only the minor expenditures which have been made but also some of the very heavy expenditures which have to be made in the Department of National Defence. We have seen vast sums of money committed to various projects. I hope those expenditures will be examined. Some of these projects are still continuing. We have commitments made to the future, and that is why it is important that there should be an examination of the expenditures made in the past.

One o'clock.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at one o'clock I was endeavouring to point out to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitiam (Mr. Regier) the reasons why this committee could be helpful in examining the expenditures which have been made during the period into which this committee is called upon to examine. I was pointing out that there were a certain number of projects which had been initiated during that period and that money had been spent on those projects but that the expenditures had not been completed because the projects were continued and therefore an examination by this committee might be very helpful. If there are any unnecessary expenditures which have been undertaken in those years and are being reflected in the future, suggestions will be appreciated by the government if they can point the way to reducing those expenditures.
May I merely point out the fact that the construction of naval vessels takes a number of years. The original allotments of money have to be made long before construction starts because long leads have to be obtained. This is also true of a great deal of electronic equipment, aircraft and so forth. Therefore I believe that an examination of the expenditures which have been made in the past would be helpful when the reasons for those expenditures are explained to the committee and the expenditures are examined in the light of the background of the reasons given. Any suggestions that would result in economies being effected would be greatly appreciated.
As I said in my opening remarks, I am sure that salutary effects can be achieved and will accrue from this examination in exactly the same way as beneficial and helpful recommendations have been made by previous committees and have been accepted after examination and review by my department. We are sincere in our efforts to cut down the amount of money which is being spent on national defence. I am very conscious of the burden which is placed on the taxpayer by these big national defence expenditures. There is nobody more anxious than I am to see the elimination of any waste, extravagance or duplication from defence expenditures.
It is quite impossible for a minister of national defence to be able to examine every item of expenditure there is and every item of administration. He has to concern himself very largely with general policy and, as all hon. members know, there are other duties he must attend. He must attend the regular

sittings of this house. He must also attend discussions and cabinet meetings affecting a wide range of subjects and therefore he is not able to devote his full time to the administration of his department.
Mr. Speaker, will my hon. friend permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any point in accepting interruptions at this point. I will not accept a question at this stage.
We have a deputy minister who is there to assist and look after the general administration. Let me say I welcome the setting up of this committee and look forward to valuable advice being given by the hon. members who will constitute that committee.
A question was raised regarding classified material. It is true that certain information is classified and there are various degrees of classification starting with what is described as top secret information all the way down to confidendial information. Much of that can be given to the committee. A lot of that classified information, I know, has been published in the press. It is a very different matter, for example, to read information in the press, no matter how reliable the journal may be, and to have this information confirmed by a minister of the crown officially. That is why one has to be very careful regarding classified information.
Much of the classified information which affects the department concerns the arrangements which are being made by other countries to meet their contribution to our agreements which might have been reached for mutual defence. It would not be right for the minister of another country to give out information about the forces, ships, aircraft and details of that kind which are being carried out by another country although that country hay have allowed what appears to be extremely reliable information to be published in the press. At the top of the range of classified information there is information of a highly secret nature which I have no right to give out to anybody who is not on the authorized list.
Some questions were asked about the gap which might exist in the information to be supplied on expenditures, it being claimed that because we were limited to those expenditures which had been declared in the public accounts the examination would be allowed to cover a period only up to March of 1959. Unless that information has been published and examined by public accounts it must still be regarded as of an interim nature. It is incomplete and has not been audited. When
National Defence
my estimates are presented either to the committee that is being set up or to the committee of the whole any hon. member can ask how much money has been spent on any particular item during the last year. That is done continually. Hon. members rise and inquire how much money was spent last year on construction or purchasing of equipment and that information is always available.
There was some query as to the dividing line between policy and administration. There is no hard and fast line drawn as between what is policy and what is administration. Broad policies connected with our external affairs, which the Department of National Defence must implement, have all been announced time and time again; but there are matters which are of a fringe or borderline nature which might perhaps be described as the policy of administration, such as the acquirement perhaps of some weapons, or something of that sort well. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made quite clear that those expenditures were to be considered in relation to the general policy, but that the general policy was not to be discussed. It is entirely up to the committee itself to decide where that line is drawn. I have explained several times that we are anxious to have this committee. We want this committee to do a job, and we shall not put any limitation on it except the general, broad limitation which is explained in the motion which we are placing before the house today, which is quite broad, quite clear. It will be up to the committee itself to decide where the dividing line between administration and policy is drawn.
With these remarks, Mr. Speaker, it only remains for me to express surprise and profound disappointment that hon. members on the other side of the house have indicated they will not co-operate with us and that they want to have this committee done away with, not to have this committee set up. They are like a bunch of spoiled children. They came out feeling that they were going to have something which they had no reason to expect, but when they find that we have gone a very long way to satisfy their request they whine and blubber because they have not got the whole thing they expected. It is, I say, with profound regret that I see this lack of co-operation on the part of the opposition.
We are going to go ahead with this committee and if the members of the opposition do not want to co-operate, we have enough talent on this side to be able to advise the minister and he will be able to draw the benefits from their advice. I repeat, I am sorry because there is limited talent on the other

National Defence
side which we could have used. I am sorry that they have expressed a determination to try and block the setting up of this committee. I again move, Mr. Speaker, that this committee be now established.
I am sorry that I interrupted the hon. member when he was speaking. Will he now permit me to ask him a question?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: As long as you do not make a speech.

The minister has said that he could not possibly be responsible for all expenditures in the department of which he is the senior minister. In view of this extraordinary statement, will he explain to the house why he does not assign that function to the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny), who by training perhaps can undertake that responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have already explained in the house what are the responsibilities of the Associate Minister of National Defence. I explained how pleased I was that he has been appointed. He has been a great help, and his particular sphere has been that of administration, as I explained to the house not very many days ago. I am sorry that the hon. member for Essex East was not here at that time, or had turned his deaf ear to the explanation I gave.
May I ask a question?
Does the hon. gentleman wish to ask a question?
I desire to ask a question of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know
whether the house wants to assume the responsibilities of a committee. It seems to me these are the type of questions which could be asked in the committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Under these terms of reference it would not be allowed in the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. If the minister says he is not willing to accept the question, I am afraid it cannot be asked.
Do I understand the minister will not accept the question?
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to take exception to a statement-
Order.
I am rising, sir, as is my right under the rules, to take exception to what I consider to be a misrepresentation of my-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member feels that he has been misinterpreted, he is quite at liberty at this stage, rather than in the middle of the speech, to make a correction.

That is what I was doing. I did not feel that I wanted to be discourteous to the minister because I did not feel he was deliberately seeking to misrepresent, but I think he did misrepresent the position I took in the estimates committee at the time it was set up when we were in office. He read certain passages from my statement at that time and applied them to this debate. The reason I felt I was misrepresented is this and I will try to put it as briefly as possible. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT ALTERNATIVE ARRANGEMENTS FOR UNIVERSITY GRANTS  EXTENSION OF INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
This resolution contemplates two amendments to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, one to provide alternative arrangements with respect to federal grants to universities and the other to extend for a further period of two years the increase which was introduced in 1958 in the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax. I should like to deal first with the amendment involving the standard rate of personal income tax.
The committee will recall that when the present government took office the standard rates specified in the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act and on which the tax rental and equalization payments were based were as follows: corporation tax, 9 per cent; individual income tax, 10 per cent;: succession duty, 50 per cent.

Necessarily it must be an estimate at this point. It will be seen from the table that the increase from 10 to 13 per cent in the standard rate of individual income tax increased the value of payments and abatements to the provinces, and of course correspondingly increased the cost to the federal treasury by $55.9 million in 1958-59, $65 million in 1959-60, and it is estimated will increase payments and abatements by $68.3 million in 1960-61. The distribution of these amounts by provinces is shown in the table I have just presented.
For the year 1960-61 it is estimated- and I stress the word "estimated'-that the increase in the standard rate of individual income tax will mean additional payments to the provinces as follows:	Newfoundland,
$1,950,000; Nova Scotia, $3,057,000; New Brunswick, $2,556,000; to Quebec in payments, $7,159,000, and in abatements to Quebec taxpayers, $14,487,000, for a total of $21,646,000; to Ontario, $25,949,000; to Manitoba, $3,822, 000; to Saskatchewan $3,891,000; to Alberta, $5,447,000.
Prince Edward Island and British Columbia derive their benefits under the stabilization formula and are the only provinces to do so. This circumstance results from the provisions of section 5 of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act which provides for payments based on what is called the "projected tax rental payment". The projected tax rental payment is simply the amount a province would have received if the payment were calculated as though the provisions of the Tax Rental Agreements Act of 1952 were still in effect. If the projected tax rental payment as calculated is greater than the amount that a province would receive from tax rental and equalization, the province is entitled to a stabilization payment to make up the difference. For Prince Edward Island the projected tax rental payment for 1960-61 is $4,675,000 or $124,000 higher than the estimated total of tax rental and equalization payments based on a standard rate of individual income tax of 13 per cent. For British Columbia the projected tax rental payment for 1960-61 is $71,975,000 or $754,000 higher than the estimated total of tax rental and equalization.
Thus far, I have spoken of the first of the amendments to the act that is contemplated in the resolution now before the committee. The other amendment proposed is completely new as far as the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act is concerned and it relates to federal payments to institutions of higher learning. Unlike the proposed in-79951-0-140
Dominion-Provincial Relations crease in the standard rate of individual income tax which represents substantial additional costs to the federal treasury, the amendment which will be proposed with respect to university grants involves no additional cost at all to the federal treasury or to the provinces. The amendment proposed will simply provide alternative arrangements so that grants now paid by the federal government to institutions of higher learning under the authority of the annual Appropriation Act can be paid out of the federal treasury through the Canadian Universities Foundation under the authority of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act or, under certain circumstances, when a province so desires directly, by that province.
Federal grants to the universities have been paid over the last nine years commencing in the fiscal year 1951-52. For the first five of these years they were paid on the basis of 50 cents per capita. For the next two years they were paid on the basis of $1 per capita; and for the last two years on the basis of $1.50 per capita of population. To the end of the present month the payments in these nine years total * the formidable sum of $112,509,238. The payments from April 1, 1952 to June 21, 1957 total $44,316,738; those from June 21, 1957 to March 31, 1960 total $68,192,500.
The grants have been allocated among the provinces strictly on the basis of population. Within each province distribution has been made among the universities on the basis of full time, intra-mural student enrolment in courses leading to degrees. Commencing in the fiscal year 1956-57 the distribution was made by the national conference of Canadian universities, and this year by its successor, the recently incorporated Canadian Universities Foundation under the terms of an agreement dated January 18, 1960 with the Minister of Finance, authorized by the Appropriation Act of 1959. Parliament has made the provision each year by an item in the estimates which accordingly found its place in the Appropriation Act. It has never before been placed on a continuing basis beyond the year to which the particular Appropriation Act applied.
At this time, Mr. Chairman, may I ask permission to insert in Hansard a table showing the amounts broken down by provinces provided by the federal government for university grants since the inception of the program?
