The federal grants are paid by the Canadian Universities Foundation only on application by the particular university. They have been welcomed by all recipient universities. They have greatly aided these institutions in their efforts to meet their financial problems in the face of the huge increase in the number of young Canadians seeking the benefit of higher education to equip them for life. Moreover, the system of grants has been accepted without challenge by the governments of the nine Englishspeaking provinces. There have been requests from the universities of Nova Scotia for a greater measure of equalization in the grants as between the universities of the different provinces, having regard to the much larger proportion of students in the population of that province than in others; but otherwise the system has met with wide approbation in nine provinces.
A very different view, however, has been taken in the province of Quebec. In the first year the grants were made available, 195152, the grants amounting to $2,027,800 were accepted by the universities of that province. In the succeeding eight years, of the qualifying educational institutions in the province of Quebec only two colleges have accepted the grants. So far as the universities and other qualifying colleges are concerned, the grants have gone unclaimed. For the four years 1952-53 to 1955-56 inclusive, they lapsed. Commencing in 1956-57 the unclaimed grants did not lapse, but under a change in the law accumulated in the hands of the national conference of Canadian universities and now the Canadian Universities Foundation. By February 29 the accumulation aggregated over $25 million. The reasons the grants were not accepted by the universities of Quebec are well known. Quebec regarded the scheme as a trespass upon the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces over education.
In the face of this situation I stated the views of the government in this house on September 6, 1958, as reported on page 4726 of Hansard as follows:
Let me make it abundantly clear, Mr. Chairman, that this government will always scrupulously respect the terms of the Canadian constitution. It is plainly recognized that education is a field of jurisdiction exclusively assigned to the provinces under the British North America Act. As long as this government is in office there will never be any attempt made to trespass on that jurisdiction exclusively vested in the provinces.

Last October 15, during the course of the dominion-provincial conference of ministers

Dominion-Provincial Relations of finance and provincial treasurers, the late Premier Paul Sauve of Quebec opened talks with the federal government on this question. Out of the extended discussions which ensued have emerged proposals by the federal government to all the provinces. These were set forth by the Prime Minister in identical letters to all provincial premiers on December 9 and made public on December 10. They are now embodied in this resolution and the legislation to follow.
Briefly, an alternative to the present system is made available to every province, whether or not it has rented the corporation tax field to the federal government. To place itself in a position to choose the new alternative system, a province which has rented this tax field to the federal government may revise its tax rental agreement and resume the collection of its own corporation tax.
Where any province which collects its own corporation tax chooses to pay additional grants to its institutions of higher learning on the basis of student enrolment on a scale equivalent to $1.50 per capita of its population, its corporate taxpayers will receive an additional abatement of 1 per cent under the Income Tax Act, raising that abatement from 9 to 10 per cent. This option will be available for the taxation years 1960 and 1961 provided a province requests amendment of its agreement with respect to the taxation year 1960 by April 30, 1960, and with respect to the taxation year 1961 by December 31, 1960.
An additional abatement of 1 per cent to corporate taxpayers has a different value in each province. In no case will it be the precise equivalent of $1.50 per capita. In some provinces the value of such an abatement is much greater than the $1.50 per capita presently paid to the Canadian Universities Foundation for institutions of higher learning, and in other provinces the yield from an additional 1 per cent tax on corporate income would be quite inadequate to finance university grants of $1.50 per capita based on total population.
At this point, I should like to ask leave to have printed in Hansard a table showing a comparison of the grants of $1.50 per capita with the yields of a 1 per cent corporation tax for the fiscal year 1960-61 for all provinces.

I cannot conclude these remarks without paying tribute to the memory of a very great Canadian, the late Hon. Paul Sauve. Though he was spared to be the prime minister of his province for but three short months, he had established himself as a leading figure in the country's public life and had made a lasting mark upon the course of Canadian history in these times. I am now going to deal-and the minister will perhaps not be too surprised at this- with the hardy annual of the Minister of Finance, the 3 per cent increment to Walter Harris' tax-equalization plan. We in this party are more satisfied with each year that passes that this government, which on every occasion in this session that it has risen to defend itself has quoted precedents from the days when we were in office, is finally in a position where it admits it has nothing better to offer in any of these fields. With respect to this field of tax sharing all the government has been able to do-and that without the consent or approval of any province but by unilateral telegrams, sent on that day in
1958 which the minister no doubt remembers-is add a little additional money precisely on the scheme which was formulated by the former minister of finance and the former prime minister, and brought into this house by Mr. Harris and opposed by the hon. gentleman who is now the Minister of Finance and described by him as incomprehensible.
We are glad that after all these years he has begun to comprehend it and to realize how very difficult it is to provide anything in this field that will satisfy everyone. But, of course, this is not what the new era was supposed to have brought in at all. I have been looking back at the prospectuses of the new era, the prospectuses that were given us by the Prime Minister in those great days of the vision in 1957. I read from the opening campaign speech at Massey Hall in Toronto on April 25, 1957:
We believe there can be no national unity in this nation until there is a realization that the federal-provincial matters have handcuffed the provinces of this nation; have denied the municipalities adequate sources of revenue; have placed the provinces and the municipalities in a position where they cannot discharge their constitutional responsibilities or permitting the necessary development in their own territorial confines of the natural resources that there are. We believe the provinces and the municipalities must have the final resources to carry out those responsibilities. We believe in the federal system of government. We believe that its preservation is essential to Canadian unity. We believe the federal system is today being challenged by the centralization complex of the St. Laurent government and that a healthy division and balance of revenues as between the federal and provincial governments must be assured.
We intend to form a government to immediately convene a dominion-provincial conference to bring about a settlement of these problems, not in the spirit of arrogant domination as displayed by the present government, but in the spirit of unity and amity and with mutual tolerance and respect.
That was the promise; that was the vision; that was the prospectus. Like many another prospectus from Bay street, the realization did not live up to the expectations; for what did we have? We had the federal-provincial conference which was called not as soon as they formed the government but in November of 1957. We had a federal-provincial conference called, and we all remember what the premier of Ontario said at that conference about Mr. St. Laurent. He did not talk about Mr. St. Laurent having any centralizing complex, or anything of that sort; he paid tribute to the courtesy and consideration which Mr. St. Laurent had shown to representatives of the provinces on every occasion on which they had ever come to Ottawa. And what is more, there were no fewer than four separate meetings, with a good many modifications made in the proposals as a result of discussions before Mr. Harris came into this house in 1956

Dominion-Provincial Relations and introduced the tax-sharing arrangements act, which we are now being asked to amend in a very minor particular. That is what was called a centralizing measure.
But where is this new federal system, this new system of unity and amity that the Prime Minister talked about, where is it? They had one meeting. They promised another in January, 1958, but what did they get in January? They got those famous telegrams with the mistakes in arithmetic that were made by the Minister of Finance. That is what they got and they were told they could take it or leave it. They were going to get a little more money, yes. Why were they going to get a little more money? I suggest that if there had been a Conservative majority in this house after the election of 1957 the provinces would not be getting any more money now than they were getting under the agreements of 1957, but there was another election coming up and something had to be done to sweeten things up for the next election. We said at that time that that was all that would ever happen. I could quote my words, and I said them again last year-
It was colossal cynicism.

I am speaking of the hon. member's colossal cynicism.

Incidentally, the first time they finally got around to having a meeting with the provinces by an odd coincidence was when parliament was meeting. Why it was possible for them to meet when parliament was meeting in 1959 and not in 1958 is something that I will leave to the minister to explain. Last year-I could read it for the minister if he would like me to; I have looked up the Hansard references; I know the minister likes me to read my old speeches over again-

time of this parliament could be saved if the minister would just bring in a bill for the whole remaining three years because he never intended to do anything else about it, anyway, but he did not accept that invitation, and this year he has brought it in for the remaining two years. The minister should let us know clearly, not only what additional amounts, as he has done today in one of the tables I understood him to table, will accrue to the provinces-he has given us an estimate only for 1960-61 and it would not be reasonable to ask him what he thinks is going to happen in 1961-62, although perhaps some of us would like to know what his views were. Or is prudent for the minister to give.

As my hon. friend from Essex East has said, or prudent for the minister to give; but I do think that we ought also to be told how much is being paid in addition to the provinces, and how much the estimate is for the years 1960 and 1961 in unconditional payments, because very large claims have been made outside the house about the tremendous increase in the payments made as a result of action taken

by the present government since it came into office. I refer to the amounts paid to the provinces. I put my questions in a very convenient form the other day, in a starred question which the minister chose to ask to have made an order for return and which I suggested to him yesterday, or the day before, it would be very desirable to have available to us in this debate.
When all is said and done, though the government is responsible to the house, we in turn are responsible to the country and the country as a whole is entitled to know precisely what is the origin of these things. There have been very large claims-the minister will be quite familiar with what I am talking about-made outside the house about what this government has done for the provinces. I think we are entitled to have that information in precise form here in the house. I endeavoured in the question as I framed it to get that information, and it does seem to me that we should have it before we are asked finally to make our judgment whether it is expedient to do what we are being asked to do here. I am not saying this is my view because it is not, but it may be the view of some that if the government's claims to generosity are justified and in view of the minister's budgetary problems, he may even be going too far from his own point of view. Nevertheless we ought to have the information, whatever it is, and it should be made available in this committee and in a form in which it can be readily understood both by members of the committee and the country generally.
Since the minister has now told us, by introducing this resolution that the government, so far as the present currency of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act is concerned, has given up any thought of putting anything in its place and that Walter Harris' law is to be the law until 1962, which is what the minister has told us today, I think the minister should give us some prognostication, perhaps a new vision, perhaps another prospectus. We know that there have been meetings with the provincial governments. We know that the meetings were related directly to this subject and I think we ought to be told what progress has been made in working out that famous scheme for allocation of taxes which not only the Prime Minister but many of his supporters when they were on this side of the house promised would be given top priority when they became the government.
It seems to me, that we ought to have the results of that famous seminar made available to us. The minister on one occasion, I believe as was the wont of this government when we 79951-0-141
Dominion-Provincial Relations referred to it on other occasions as a seminar, said that it was established by the previous government. It is true that the previous government did establish a continuing committee to act within the terms of the broad policies laid down by their respective governments but as nearly as we could gather from the rather confused and confusing statements made by the minister about his famous seminar it was expected to generate ideas itself, to produce a new policy which would bring about that state of harmony that the Prime Minister forecast when he spoke in Massey Hall on that great occasion when he opened his triumphant campaign in 1957.
I say that we should be told whether the government really thinks that it is going to find something to substitute for the taxsharing arrangements act before 1962 or whether in fact the minister, as a result of the maturity and wisdom that he has developed in nearly three years of office, has now come to the conclusion that there was a good deal of wisdom in the views expressed in 1956 by those people who had had the longest experience in this field, who had discussed the matter for years and discussed it on a basis, as Mr. Frost said, of the greatest courtesy and consideration, with the provincial governments.
This is, I suppose, in a fundamental way, the basic problem of our country. It may not be the most important immediate problem. I am not going to continue in this vein, Mr. Chairman, so you do not need to look anxious. I think the most immediate current problem is, of course, the unemployment problem, but of the basic fundamental problems of the country, surely, the most important is finding the kind of financial basis which will, in the words, of the Prime Minister, ensure what we all want, the maintenance of a federal and not a unitary system of government.
That was, of course, precisely what Mr. Mackenzie King and Mr. Ilsley started out to do at the end of the war when the legislation was proposed and discussed in a conference which was the parent and precursor of the legislation that the minister is now asking us to amend. At all stages throughout all of that period the purpose was to put the provincial governments in a position where they could carry out their functions themselves and would have enough financial capacity to do so because, as Mr. Bracken, who I am sure will be regarded by the Minister of Finance as a great authority, said at the famous federal-provincial conference in 1941, provincial autonomy without the means to support it is an arid and empty thing. I lived on the prairies in the 30's when we had provincial autonomy without the means

Dominion-Provincial Relations to support it and I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that everything about the prairies in those days was pretty arid.
It was this great problem that the Liberal party set out to solve as soon as they came into office in 1935, and we cannot help taking some satisfaction from the fact that, after three years of office, the present administration has not been able to find a single deviation from that solution. We are very glad that they feel so flush that they can pay a little more money but that has not changed the formula. That has not changed that situation which the Prime Minister described in Massey Hall as this centralizing complex of the St. Laurent government. The same law is here. It was never a centralizing law at all; it was a decentralizing law.
Oh, oh.

Why are hon. gentlemen keeping it on the statute books if they do not agree? Why do they not vote against it? The plain fact is that they know perfectly well why Mr. Duplessis agreed to take the equalization payment after the amendment of 1956. Why did he take it? Because that very large sum of about $60 million paid from the federal treasury into the treasury of Quebec without any conditions attached was what enabled the provincial government to carry on, and without it they could not have carried on. Without it their autonomy in 1958 would have been as sterile as the autonomy of the prairies was in the 30's. It was saved by that $60 million which they started to take and which they are still taking and which I am very glad they are taking.
I think it was tragic that after so many years there was not equalization right across the country. I think it was the greatest of all the great achievements of the St. Laurent government in the domestic field to establish a system of tax sharing which does give to the provincial governments, regardless of their tax base, a sufficient assured income to maintain provincial services without having to surrender any of their functions to the federal government.
In 1936 and 1937 when the Rowell commission was beginning its work there were two possible ways of dealing with the problem. One was to transfer many of the functions of the provinces to parliament here and finance them that way and the other was to put the provinces in a position to finance them themselves.
The government of Mr. Mackenzie King, the government of Ernest Lapointe and the government of P. J. A. Cardin made the basic decision that they were for provincial rights

and that what they would do was to work out some scheme to put the provinces in a position to do their own financing for themselves and treat the people equally from one end of this country to the other. That is something that should never be forgotten.
It would have been very easy to go in the other direction. In fact, the Bennett government started in the other direction. By some of that legislation which the courts found to be ultra vires they had started in the direction of centralization, in the direction of trying to gather up provincial functions here in Ottawa. Incidentally, I may say that one of the members of that Bennett government was a gentleman who, for many years, was provincial treasurer in the government of Mr. Duplessis.
I just recall this past history because we have had so much distortion of it over the last few years and only as recently as yesterday in the main editorial in the Ottawa Journal, which perhaps may have been the mainspring of what I am saying this afternoon. But the plain fact is, Mr. Chairman, that this tax sharing plan which the minister is now asking us to amend in order to make it a little bit more generous to the provinces was a great achievement in three ways. It was a great contribution to provincial autonomy in this country; it was a great contribution to equality of opportunity and to equality of service for all Canadians, no matter in what province they live. For those two reasons it is proving to be a great contribution to the unity of Canada.
As to approving the extra 3 per cent that is being offered for two more years by the present government or will be offered in the bill it proposes to introduce, we are of course in favour of that provision. We supported it in 1958 and in 1959 and we support it again. But before we reach a final decision on this matter I think we should have before us the kind of factual information that I indicated earlier it would desirable to have in order to give this matter the kind of consideration which it seems to me it is necessary for us to give in a responsible way.
I am not saying that I shall not have something more to say before the committee has completed its deliberations but I want to say once again, in order to emphasize the point, that we on this side of the chamber are extremely proud of two things. We are extremely proud of the fact that the taxsharing arrangements act is standing the test of time and is standing it very well. We are also proud indeed that the great vision of Louis St. Laurent in connection with

the university grants is now going to come to fruition from one end of Canada to the other.
Under a Conservative government.

First of all, Mr. Chairman,
I must say that I enjoyed the extremely interesting speech made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. 1 think everyone will agree that his speech gave evidence of his particular training in three fields. From listening to him carefully-and I say this seriously-I think we had evidence of his training as an historian, as a barrister and solicitor and, shall I say, of his work as chief propagandist for the Liberal party. However, other than that, I thought it was a most interesting speech and an informative one.
In pursuing the few remarks I wish to make on behalf of this group, I want to say that I join with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the minister in their tribute to the former premier of Quebec whose death unfortunately came so soon. I think he made a great contribution to this good work during the short time he was able to act as premier of his province.
We in this group try to be fair. We recognize the good work that was done by the former prime minister, namely Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, in strengthening and developing national unity in Canada and in giving effect to pieces of legislation that were the first steps toward grants to universities and that provided the funds necessary for Canadian provinces, shall I say, to experience the reality of Canadian autonomy because they were able to do so under proper financial circumstances.
However, I must bring to the attention of the committee the fact that these grants to universities are only a partial implementation of the policy that has been advocated by members of this party since its formation in 1932. That policy is federal aid to education on a broadly based scale so that every child in Canada, regardless of where it lives or of the economic circumstances of its parents, should have an equal opportunity to secure the education of which it is capable of taking full advantage.
This payment is one aspect of that policy, and we trust that it will be of such assistance to the universities in Quebec that it will benefit young men and young women in the province of Quebec who would not otherwise benefit were this arrangement not completed. We are delighted to know that the universities in Quebec are to enjoy the benefits of this resolution, which benefits have been enjoyed 79951-0-141J

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am indeed delighted with the opportunity to take part in this debate, not only as a member of parliament but as a former teacher.
The matter we are now considering has long made headlines, not only in the province of Quebec but throughout Canada.
This is the most significant issue we have had to face in this house. It is a problem which is vital for the survival of our universities, for our young people of today and also vital for the safeguard of our rights and prerogatives.
In saying that the problem is a vital one for our young people, I should like to endorse a statement made in 1878 by the Hon. Mr. Parent, when he said:
It would be a grievous mistake to assume that peace can be restored to mankind by purely economic methods, just by feeding the poor if, at the same time, we do not provide for the needs and the rights of the mind.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
As I said just now, Mr. Chairman, I believe the problem is of the utmost significance, and I am sorry I was unable to prepare myself to deal with it adequately. I shall, nevertheless, try to explain to the house the quite justified and legitimate feeling of Quebec.
There has been for many years a struggle between Ottawa and Quebec. Each proclaimed its rights and if we read some excerpts of a brief submitted by the Montreal chamber of commerce, we will find this:
As far as corporate income tax is concerned, the chamber of commerce of the Montreal district feels it is its duty to confirm the recommendations made with regard to individual income tax. The corporation, like the individual, should be left a minimum necessary to its expansion and survival, and equality of sacrifice should in all cases be observed.
The chamber of commerce of the district of Montreal believes that these principles should be recognized by setting up progressive rates once the basic exemptions are established.
The chamber of commerce of the district of Montreal also believes for instance, that any corporation aware of its responsibilities to society, should be granted the privilege of contributing of its own free will, and according to its wishes and means, to various social, charitable and educational organizations.
The chamber of commerce also said the following:
In the view of the chamber of commerce of the district of Montreal, it is generally agreed that educational and cultural institutions should be able to count on the state to supplement their budgets.
However, the chamber of commerce of the district of Montreal cannot admit that, disregarding the Canadian constitution, the federal state should subsidize cultural and educational institutions by means of direct grants, though it may and does indeed recognize that they are under provincial jurisdiction.
Federal authorities do not seem to have found my other solution to this permanent provincial problem than financial aid by the central government.
Such a solution can definitely be only a temporary one and, in spite of all the precautions that were taken to safeguard constitutional integrity, it cannot be approved.
In this field as in all others, the chamber of commerce of the district of Montreal cannot accept any solution directly or indirectly implying any subordination of the provincial governments to the federal government in those fields where its jurisdiction is exclusive.
Before dealing any further with this resolution, I want to make a few retrospective remarks with regard to events since 1952.
A few moments ago, I noted the words of praise spoken by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for our great man the late Paul Sauve.
I also heard the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), speak-

ing of Mr. St. Laurent, whom I greatly respect but whose principles I cannot share.
Indeed Quebec cannot be deprived of its rights and prerogatives, and when the then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, advocated an extreme form of federalism, he acted in opposition to the very letter of the constitution which protects Quebec provincial rights and prerogatives.
Mr. Chairman, I also have to pay tribute to to a great man who is no more, one never much appreciated or loved by our opponents because they were not successful against him. I am referring to the hon. Mr. Maurice Du-plessis, who, all his life, fought for his province of Quebec and devoted himself to the safeguard and maintenance of our rights and prerogatives. It was here in Ottawa, I believe, that he said, during the 1955 conference:
Co-operation with the Ottawa government, yes; assimilation, never.
And that is what he did. He never wanted to be party to a policy whose purpose was to surrender to Ottawa the rights and privileges which were given us by the fathers of confederation.
Surely I cannot congratulate a government which has sacrificed everything, but I must pay tribute to the one who, in keeping with his vocation, has defended the rights which are recognized by the constitution. And if we can now enjoy those rights, it is due to the man who always refused to accept the proposals of the federal government in office at that time. That must not be forgotten, and it must be recognized that he was, both for the province of Quebec and for Canada as a whole, a great Canadian, a great patriot.
Mr. Chairman, also recalled during those conferences, were the words of a great Canadian who was, I admit, a member of the Liberal party, a party which has included men of principles, men who would never have agreed to grasp anything belonging to the provinces. Indeed, there were people of that type, and I could name some of them.
Mr. Chairman, I could mention the name of a great patriot, a Liberal, the hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who said, in 1887:
It Is an absolutely false principle which claims that one government can collect revenue while another one spends it.
More than forty years later, the fundamental truth appeared even more obvious, when the hon. Mr. MacKenzie King, heir of Mr. Laurier's policy, stated in 1929, in the House of Commons, that rights belonging to provinces should not be tampered with.

And earlier, in 1884, there was also the Hon. Honore Mercier who stated:
The provinces existed before the dominion (Canada), and it is from them that the dominion got its powers. The provinces are sovereign within the limits of their attributes, and any interference with that sovereignty is a violation of the federal pact.
Well, Mr. Chairman, those men belonged to the Liberal party, to the great Liberal party of days gone by, for which I had great admiration. I would have liked its successors to follow in the footsteps of those great patriots like Laurier, King and Mercier. But such was not the case.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier was born in L'Assomption, in my constituency.

Mr. Chairman, I believe that after the speech we have just heard, it would be in order for me to read again to the committee the resolution which is now before the house. It reads as follows:


That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act to provide certain alternative arrangements for payment, either by Canada through the Canadian Universities Foundation or directly by a province, of the grants to institutions of higher learning presently paid under the authority of the Appropriation Act; and also to extend for a further period of two years the rate of 13 per cent for standard individual income tax for the purpose of calculating the tax equalization payments to the provinces and the amounts payable to the provinces under the tax rental agreements.
I agree with the Minister of Finance, that this resolution can be considered from two different angles, the first one deals with the extension for a period of two years of the arrangements as they exist today; the second one dealing with new arrangements that the minister has explained and about which I would like to say a word.
However, Mr. Chairman, like my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), and the minister himself, I would like to tell the house that we, in the opposition, agree with him about the great qualities of the late Hon. Paul Sauve, the great former premier of the province of Quebec. We believe that had Providence not taken his life, he would have brought along, I am sure, a greater unity between the various provinces which form our country. Personally, Mr. Chairman, I think so and for more than one reason. I am convinced of it. I believe his idea of politics was similar to that of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent and that in many regards his conduct appeared to be based on and patterned after that of the former prime minister of Canada.
I believe also that it was his intention, at least according to the letters he wrote and to his policy during the short period he was premier of the province of Quebec, to take his province out of the isolation in which the Union Nationale had placed it, in order to give it greater expansion within the Canadian confederation. That is why I say, as did the Minister of Finance, that the Hon. Paul Sauve, the former premier of Quebec, wanted to give his province greater expansion within the Canadian confederation, and had he lived, no doubt he would have achieved this.
Mr. Chairman we have just heard the speech of the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. English), who, in his remarks not only played politics, but appeared to have no knowledge of the basis on which provincial relations have been established under the government of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent.

I believe it is important, at this time, to remind the house that in 1956, an agreement was reached between the federal and provincial governments, which came into force in 1957, and which gave the provinces the choice between leasing or not leasing their taxation powers to the federal government, as they wished. They had the choice in three fields: (1) in the field of personal income tax; (2) in the field of corporation tax; (3) in the field of succession duties. Under this agreement, eight provinces of Canada decided to rent their powers. The province of Ontario leased its powers with regard to personal income tax, but retained taxation powers on corporation and estate income tax. The province of Quebec did not lease anything. Therefore, it was free to impose taxes under those arrangements. Thus, there was no interference at all in the provincial field, contrary to what was stated a moment ago by the hon. member for Gaspe. An important feature of this arrangement is that whether the provinces lease their taxation fields or not, they are not granted any privileges and suffer no discrimination. They suffered no detriment. They themselves collect what others get as the price of rental. Like the others they also receive equalization payments.
But the St. Laurent formula, a unique formula, the 13-9-50 formula, which the minister has mentioned earlier is obviously not a perfect one but no other party, no other government has been able to find a better one.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That is the formula which, after having been many a time considered seriously and conscientiously by the former prime minister, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent and by the previous government, was found to be the best in the circumstances. So far, as was said a moment ago by my good friend, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, it has not been possible to find a better formula. All that has been done to this day has been to take the formula, and to extend its provisions to include a further 3 per cent.
Therefore, I say again that, under that formula which the hon. member for Gaspe claims is unfair-if he did not say so directly, he implied it-the province of Quebec has received between $50 million and $60 million in equalization payments. Furthermore in the estimates which the Minister of Finance
Dominion-Provincial Relations introduced in this house for the fiscal year 1960-61, it is indicated that the province of Quebec will receive some $66 million under those equalization payments. It therefore follows that the formula is not so bad, but, on the contrary, a good one. May I briefly tell you what the formula means, in order to prove once more that it involves no invasion of the provincial field.
Under that formula, the federal government says three things: "First of all, if you rent your powers, I shall give you in return the yield of those three taxation rates. Second, if you do not rent them, I shall reduce my federal taxes by those three percentages in your province. Third, as I know that the yield of those three taxes per capita varies considerably from one province to another, and that, in the poorest provinces, they are a source of discrimination, I shall offer you without any strings attached grants that will equalize the revenues from those taxes in the various provinces, taking as a basis the two wealthiest provinces, that is, Ontario and British Columbia.
That formula, therefore, does not involve any interference; each party remains on its positions, and keeps its powers. Then, how can we say, in all sincerity, in all fairness, that there is interference in the provincial field. Besides, those who claim that there is interference, why do they not prove it? How is it that they did not submit the matter to the courts to prove that there is interference? They did not do so. And if they did not do so, we are perfectly right in saying emphatically that the formula is fair, that it is the best formula which could have been developed under the circumstances. I have therefore no hesitation in saying that this formula does not involve any interference in the provincial field.
Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of dealing with the second part of this resolution, because my hon. friend the member for Bonavista-Twillingate handled that very well.
However, in relation to the first part of the resolution which the Minister of Finance emphasized, in order to give us a few details -not all of them, of course, because we shall get them, no doubt, when the bill is submitted to the house-I should like to call the attention of the house to a letter written by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefen-baker) to the then premier of the province of Quebec. That letter was tabled in the house after an inquiry for return by mem-

Dominion-Provincial Relations bers of the opposition. At this stage, I should like to quote a part only of that letter, which is dated December 22, 1959:
Should the Quebec legislature decide to accept the new formula, and should the federal act be amended by parliament as proposed by the government, the result will be that in the next two fiscal years, that is from April 1, 1960 to March 31, 1962, the following provisions will take effect.
Mr. Chairman, here are the three provisions to which I wish to call the house's particular attention:
(a)	Should the Quebec legislature decide to raise the provincial corporation tax to 10 per cent or more of corporate profits, there shall be granted to corporations affected by that tax a 10 per cent exemption in lieu of the present 9 per cent on the federal tax on corporate profits;
(b)	The $1.50 per capita grant paid to universities by the federal government, with the authorization of parliament shall be cut off with respect to universities in the province of Quebec.
(c)	The difference between the yield of the additional tax exemption of 1 per cent and the $1.50 per capita exemption for your province shall be adjusted, so that the tax position of the federal government will remain unchanged. In other words, should the 1 per cent tax exemption be greater than an amount equal to $1.50 per capita, as will be the case, the federal government will deduct the amount in excess of the equalization payment which is now being paid to the province of Quebec out of federal funds under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act. As an example, assuming the new formula were applied on the basis of 1959 figures, the federal treasury would lose and the provincial treasury gain approximately $9,250,000 as a result of the change in corporation tax rates. On the other hand, grants to universities based on the figure of $1.50 per capita would amount to $7,500,000 in the case of the province of Quebec; the difference of $1,750,000 would be deducted from the equalization payment for the province of Quebec, which in 1959 will amount to approximately $67,000,000.
Mr. Chairman, this letter which was sent to the former premier of the province of Quebec by the Prime Minister of Canada prompts me to ask a number of questions of the Minister of Finance.
In view of the three paragraphs I just read, would the province of Quebec have to distribute the yield on the basis of $1.50 per capita?
Would the province of Quebec have to refund the excess of that tax to the federal government, if the yield were greater than $1.50 per capita?
Moreover, should there be a deficit, as I understand from the letter written by the Prime Minister of Canada, will the payment made by the federal government not represent a federal subsidy for education purposes.


Mr. Chairman, those are questions which I think the Minister of Finance ought to deal with either in the resolution stage, or when the bill comes up for second reading.
Finally, if the minister agrees to answer these questions, would he tell us also if, under these circumstances, the province of Quebec would not become the fiscal agent, for its own purposes, of the federal government? In short, the question I ask the Minister of Finance is this: Does he think that the new formula-which, unfortunately, we will not know entirely before reading the bill-is better than the one which existed under the arrangements that the minister is seeking to amend now?
Mr. Chairman, I believe we have a right to such answers. Obviously, we, the members of the opposition, cannot at this time consider wholly and fairly the results of these amendments before we have read the bill. However, we are happy to hear that a formula has been found. In fact, we believe, as Mr. St. Laurent believed at the time, that in the present circumstances, the universities are increasingly in need of financial aid. The universities of the province of Quebec, like those of the other provinces, need capital to realize the technical, scientific and other developments they wish to undertake in their institutions, just as the classical colleges of the province of Quebec also need it.
That is why I can say in this house that we, of the Liberal party, shall support the principles of the resolution in order to be able, at the second reading, to get all the details of the formula.
Mr. Chairman, I come back to the questions that I put a moment ago to the Minister of Finance. I feel that it is his duty to answer those questions prompted by the Prime Minister's letter to the then premier of the province of Quebec. If those questions are answered, then when I have the opportunity to do so, I shall be able to take a more definite stand at the second reading of the bill.

Mr. Chairman, allow me at the outset to say that I share entirely the views of previous speakers, including the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) with regard to the Hon. Paul Sauve, whom we all remember so vividly.
I knew him personally for a long time. I was on very friendly terms with him, and the

last time I saw him, it was about a month before his death. He talked with me for an hour of various problems of concern to him, and of the matter under consideration at present.
He had an acute sense of realism and a deep respect for the constitution.
He was also very eager to co-operate and the measure introduced today by the Minister of Finance proves it to a degree.
In my turn, I want to say how very much affected I was by his death, and that we shall forever remember his imperishable achievements in our province.
Mr. Chairman, the legislation now before us is, as all will easily understand, of vital interest for the province of Quebec. Of course, it is meant for all provinces, but having to face the facts, it is of special interest to Quebec, because, in 1951, the Liberal government thought it appropriate to subsidize universities. Since then the province of Quebec did not take advantage of those grants, for reasons to which I shall probably refer again in the course of the few remarks I intend to make.
The proposed legislation therefore gives the provinces a choice between the present state of affairs, or a deduction from corporation taxes which will be raised from 9 to 10 per cent in the case of provinces that prefer to subsidize our Canadian universities on their own.
To my mind, Mr. Chairman, the deduction principle is a very happy one.
Last year, I had the opportunity-as I also did during my election campaign-to say how much I had admired the gesture of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent who, after having found opposition in Quebec, and being aware that this opposition was due to a firm wish to observe the constitution, agreed, after a meeting with the Hon. Maurice Duplessis, to increase from 5 to 10 per cent the individual income tax deduction, so that provinces wishing to do so, and more particularly the province of Quebec, might exercise their own jurisdiction in the taxation field.
It is the same principle which is now at the basis of this resolution, a principle according to which Quebec will itself get the money which it needs to finance its universities. These, I repeat, come under the exclusive jurisdiction of each province of Canada.

The report of the subcommittee of the committee of the other place in connection with this particular case has a great number of oddities in it and strange circumstances which I think bear relating before the committee comes to a decision as to whether or not to report the bill.
I will start at the outset and say that in this instance it is one of those cases in which children are involved. Apparently there are two children in their teens or something of that nature, although their ages are not given, and one of a younger age. It is also the type of case in which investigators, so-called, are witnesses before the committee, even though they are not called investigators. They classify themselves, one as an administrator and one as a salesman. In this instance the husband, according to the evidence, deserted his wife in 1947.
I think a reference or two to this matter is in order because I think it has quite a substantial bearing upon the consideration that should be given by this committee to the granting of this particular divorce or the petition. In order to have this matter clear, I am referring to page 10 of the Senate committee evidence. The question is asked of the petitioner by Mr. Ralph A. Cohen, a lawyer in the city of Montreal. Mr. Cohen asks the petitioner a number of other questions then he asks this one:
Q. And then your husband deserted you in 1947. Did you hear from him after that?
A. No.
Q. Did you hear from him from time to time?
A. Just from Christmas until about March.
Q. Of 1948?
A. 1948, yes.
There are a couple of other incidental questions following that relating to the parents of the respondent and so on but another subsequent question is as follows:
Q. Since the time of your husband's desertion have you ever seen him since let us say 1947 until today?
A. No.
I submit that while adultery is supposed to be the ground for divorce or perhaps I should qualify that statement and say circumstances that would reasonably lead one to assume that adultery might take place is normally considered as ground for divorce, in this particular adultery had nothing to do with it whatsoever. These are not the grounds that were considered or given weight but other grounds and other circumstances were given more consideration-and I think properly so-and I think this committee should give more consideration to those things than it does to the question of adultery.
I am of the opinion that in this instance more consideration or more weight was attached to the question of desertion having

been in existence for some 12 years or 13 years now and to cruelty. In my opinion those were the things that were given consideration and I think this committee should give them some consideration. Incidentally, I think our general law as it applies to divorce should be extended so that divorce can be based on such grounds as desertion or cruelty. I suggest that in this instance those are factors which should be considered. From the evidence found at pages 10 and 11 there is reference to the question of the attitude of the husband toward his wife during the years prior to their splitting up or prior to his desertion. I submit that if we read the evidence carefully here we shall discover that cruelty is one factor to which we can properly give some weight. The question is asked again by Mr. Cohen of the petitioner:
Q. Could you tell this committee some of the reasons why you are petitioning for a divorce?
That is a fairly clear question. We all know there is only one reason why you petition for a divorce or one basis upon which you place it and that is adultery or circumstances which would allow one to come to the conclusion that adultery might take place. Mr. Cohen asks this question:
Q. Could you tell this committee some of the reasons why you are petitioning for a divorce? I understand you lived with your husband for about 10 or 12 years?
A. Because of his drinking, gambling, running around, coming home and throwing things around.
Q. Did he ever leave for periods of time?
A. Yes.
Q. Did he ever tell you where he had gone?
A. No.
Q. Did he ever show any interest in your three daughters?
A. Very little.
Q. Did he from the time he deserted you until today send any money for your support?
A. No.
Q. How do you get along?
A. Needing mothers' allowance.
Following that there are some questions by Senator Bradley on page 11 directed toward the same thing. The questions by the senator are as follows:
Q. Did he ever use violence towards you, or anything of that kind?
A. Yes.
Q. What did he do?
A. Well, he hit me. Is that what you mean?
Q. Yes.
A. Threw things at me, and came home and threw electric lamps around through the house.
I submit that is another instance of cruelty, the admission that he hit her and the admission in her statement in the earlier part of her evidence that he was throwing things around, drinking, gambling and so on which are part of the question of cruelty. It is to these grounds that the committee of the other house probably gave a great deal of consideration,

I think, more so than to the question of adultery. I think we must do this to because, even though there are some three pages of evidence by the administrator and the salesman who were witnesses on behalf of the petitioner as to what they had discovered, there is no reference to adultery.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that on reading it through carefully you will find the evidence is very vague and loose; and if they were to have appeared before a court I am sure the court would have inquired in much more detail as to what they had discovered.
I might add at this point that the respondent was in Winnipeg and the petitioner lived in, I think it was, the city of Quebec. In any event she lived in the province of Quebec and the respondent was in Winnipeg. I think that allows for some other comments which we will engage in in just a moment.
To show that there was not too much consideration on the part of the investigators as to whether adultery took place I think we can make reference to the evidence on page 13. The committee will recall, I am sure, that in other cases it is quite the practice for the investigator or the witness on behalf of the petitioner to give an explanation in evidence to the committee to show that there were a certain number of bedrooms, or that only one bed had been used apparently by two people, and to make reference to the number of beds, and so on. In this particular evidence even though, as I say, it runs to some three pages, which is more than in the majority of these cases, there is no reference,	not	only	to whetherthere were any	beds	but	also	as to howmany bedrooms	there	were, or	how manycouches, and so	on, in	the	particular apartment the investigators visited and within which they discovered the respondent and the co-respondent.
Quoting from the evidence to indicate what they said with respect to this particular apartment, apparently they went to the address, they then stated the address and then this question was asked:
Q. Who answered the door?
A. He answered the door.
I assume that means the respondent.
Q. Was there anyone else present in that apartment?
A. He is the one that answered the phone, but actually we walked in, and he introduced her as his wife.
-with no immediate reference before that as to anybody else being there.
Q. Did you go into that apartment?
A. Yes, we went in.
Q. Could you describe to this committee what Mr. Vaillancourt looks like, what would be his age?

Q. How was he dressed?
A. He had striped pyjamas, and a blue housecoat, sort of dark bluish housecoat.
Q. Who else was present in the apartment?
A. There was another lady with him. He said, "I would like you to meet Mrs. Vaillancourt."
So apparently the respondent introduced the lady who was there as his wife.
Q. That woman he said was Mrs. Vaillancourt, was she the petitioner?
A. No.
Then he describes the corespondent, her approximate weight and height, and things of that nature. The evidence continues:
Q. How was she dressed?
A. Bluish housecoat, sort of double-breasted thing.
I assume he is making reference to the housecoat there. Here is the important and relevant part I submit, Mr. Chairman:
Q. Did you make a survey of the apartment?
A. Yes. I asked him very politely where the bathroom was, and he showed me-and a nice living room; and I asked him the price he paid for rent there because I was interested in real estate and he showed me around, and there she was in the bathroom at the time combing her hair; she came out afterwards.
Q. Did you ask her her name?
A. Yes, I asked her her name.
Q. What was her name?
A. She said her name was Marion Caswell or Casselman or something like that.
This is an important factor to which I intend to make reference later on when we consider whether or not any arrangement was made in this particular case. Because in one instance she is introduced as a person having one name, and the next moment she says, in effect, no, that is not her name, it is something else. You will see from reading this particular reference that this is all about -the apartment itself. The rest is about what they did when they left and when they came back, and so on. There is no reference whatsoever in the evidence submitted about the couple in Winnipeg as to whether, even though they said they were man and wife, there were a number of bedrooms in the apartment, whether they slept in different beds, the same beds, or what. There is not one shred of evidence to the slightest degree.
I say that they are stretching the point a great deal in saying from the evidence given that adultery took place or could have taken place. There is no indication that this lady actually lived in that apartment with the respondent. There is no indication that she might not have lived in another apartment across the hall and was over visiting, combing her hair in the bathroom. This could well occur, we do not know. It is not clear from here what the circumstances were.

The only circumstances are that two people were in an apartment dressed in dark bluish housecoats, and things of that nature. I submit it is quite common in apartment houses to see people wandering about in housecoats. They feel properly dressed when wearing them. Many of them wear them to protect their good dress clothes which they have on underneath, or for doing housework around the home. Wearing a housecoat does not mean you have just got out of bed or intend to get into bed. There is not one shred of evidence at all of adultery and only the loosest indication-

Q. Who else was present in the apartment?

-giving his last name. Would not that be the evidence my hon. friend is looking for?

I read that evidence and pointed out, as my hon. friend has just said, that he introduced this person as his wife. But later on there is some reference, and I may as well deal with this now, as to whether she accepted that name or objected to it. It is contradictory evidence. On the last page, page 15, this question is asked of the other witness by Senator Bradley:
Q. He Introduced her as Mrs. Vaillancourt and she accepted that name?
A. She did.
But we find on page 13, about half way down, a question by Mr. Cohen to another Mr. Cohen, who is the investigator-they had the same names-to this effect:
Q. Did you ask her her name?
A. Yes, I asked her her name.
Q. What was her name?
A. She said her name was Marion Caswell or Casselman or something like that.
That is no indication that because one person introduced another as Mrs. Vaillancourt that she was. One could come to the conclusion it is quite possible that this situation did exist, that they were living together as man and wife. But apart from this there is not the least bit of evidence as to bedrooms, beds, or anything like that, except that they did put scotch tape over the door, and as a result of placing it there and seeing it there next morning they came to the conclusion that the couple did not leave the apartment on that day.
Another question which I submit should be considered is that of payment. In many cases we find that the petitioner was asked to say

who is paying for the divorce, because apparently that has some bearing on whether or not a divorce would be granted. In this instance it appears that no such question was asked, and the committee is entitled to wonder where the money in respect of this payment comes from. We are entitled to assume that more costs are involved here with respect to the remuneration of the investigators than would normally be involved. Usually the investigators have these things so well organized that they can discover their evidence within a day or two. In this case, however, the investigators spent a great deal of time and made many inquiries before they were successful. According to the evidence as it appears half way down page 12, Mr. Cohen stated:
Previous to that we searched for Mr. Vaillan-court all summer practically, and had a hard time finding him. We called on his father on St. Denis Street, Montreal, and his brother on Delorimier Ave., Montreal, and they wouldn't tell us the address, but we pestered them for so long and so often, we went to the Stewart Biscuit company-
Eventually the investigators got the address in Winnipeg. It is a fact that the more time the investigators spend on a case the higher is the cost. I would point out, also, that there are two return air trips from Montreal to Winnipeg on the part of the investigators I believe they flew out to Winnipeg aboard a Canadian Pacific Air Lines plane. It does not say here how they came back, so I think we can assume that they flew back. Even if they did not fly back, but returned by train, it would still be an expensive journey. All these costs are reflected in the charges paid by the petitioner who is asking for the divorce.
I do not like to be facetious about this, but I would gather from reading the evidence that the province of Quebec paid for the divorce in this particular case, because the petitioner was getting along on mothers' allowance. She was not working, but out of her mothers' allowance the expenses of the divorce were met. So, in effect, it was the province who paid those expenses. That is the assumption. However, I submit that this mothers' allowance could not be sufficient to defray the expenses of two investigators on an air trip from Montreal to Winnipeg and, in this case, spending the summer looking for somebody and interviewing people in order to obtain an address. These services are not provided gratis. This is a costly process, so we are entitled to ask the question: who is paying for this divorce. If the question of who pays for a divorce is an important factor, we need to know who is paying the fees and expenses of these investigators and the private bill fees in the other place. If the wrong
