person pays these charges and makes arrangements for them, the committee is entitled to know about it.
I am going to suggest that there was some arrangement made in this case in this respect. I am going to suggest that the respondent and the investigators were probably a party to it, because when they got to Winnipeg they went across the street and had a cup of coffee in a drug store and then-I am quoting from the evidence of William Cohen:
I phoned Mr. Vaillancourt's number and there was no answer. I phoned about an hour later and there was an answer, and I asked if we could see him, and he asked what it was for. I said it was rather private, I would like to discuss it myself if we could call on him. He didn't mind, he said. He was very nice about it.
Then after getting into this apartment to discuss this very private matter they spent almost an hour there; they "sat around for almost an hour and talked about the weather and how we liked Winnipeg." That is stretching things quite a bit. If two people fly from Montreal to Winnipeg and telephone a person whom they do not know with regard to a very private matter which they then discuss with him in private, I suggest it is asking the committee to accept a good deal of nonsense to expect it to believe that they just sat around and talked about the weather for an hour. I submit that if they sat around for an hour they talked about what arrangements they had made and how the divorce was going to go through so well, and that as soon as they got back the divorce would be obtained without too much difficulty.
I have already mentioned the mix-up in the names. One moment this lady is introduced as Mrs. Vaillancourt and the next moment she is introduced under some other name. This, again, is strange because you do not introduce a person to strangers as having one name, when they want to come up to ask about something in private, and then say a moment later that she has another name, and that you are living clandestinely. If that were done, I suggest it was because the lady knew who the investigators were and because they were probably no more strangers to her than you and I.
Though I submit there is no grounds for granting this divorce on the basis of adultery, I do think-and this certainly as far as I am concerned should be the law, anyway-that there is ample grounds for granting one on the basis of desertion and cruelty, both of which have been admitted, both of which are in evidence and both of which occurred. I suppose that strictly speaking we should not pass this bill on grounds on which legally we have no right to consider

Private Bills-Divorce
it, but I think we should give due weight to these matters. I believe there are ample grounds-ample moral grounds-for a divorce in this case, and I add that this is to be regretted, even if the evidence has been manufactured in order to prove something which did not take place-should this have occurred-and I submit that is the situation in this particular case.
There are some other factors in this case which could be discussed, but I see that my 30 minutes have come close to an end, and I had better leave my comments at that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I would assume that hon. members are very interested in some of the aspects of this divorce application, because I think it is unique. Certainly, it is unique in my understanding of divorce bills passing through this house.
The hon. member for Skeena has pointed out that there are a number of statements attached to this case which cannot possibly be true. He also pointed out that in this case the federal parliament is being asked to pass a private bill which is being financed by the province of Quebec. That seems to be a very odd state of affairs, to say the least. If the province of Quebec is going to continue to finance divorce cases in Ottawa the province could set up its own court and would probably find it cheaper to do so than supplying money to deserted women in that jurisdiction through the welfare branch. The money paid to the Senate for this divorce could be returned to the province of Quebec. We do not have to take money from the province which it could spend in a better way.
The hon. member for Halifax said that no adultery was proved in this case. We are therefore asked to grant the divorce solely on the grounds of desertion. I believe desertion should be one of the grounds on which divorce is granted-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. We are not
discussing methods of granting divorce but are discussing this bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Adultery has not been proved so I assume the divorce if granted will be granted on the grounds of desertion. I am in favour of granting divorce on those grounds but those grounds are not usually acceptable in these cases. The Senate feels that adultery should be indicated if not proved. In this case an attempt was made to show a common law relationship but no adultery was proved.
The question of domicile arises in this case. Because some of us are not lawyers it is necessary for us to find out what these terms mean. The third item of the petitioner's prayer reads as follows:

3. That at the time of the said marriage your petitioner and the said Charles Edward Vail-lancourt were domiciled in Canada, and have ever since continued to be and are now domiciled in Canada, in the province of Quebec.
We all know from the evidence they are not domiciled in the province of Quebec. They must be domiciled there for the divorce to be granted. It is argued that a married woman takes the domicile of her husband.
Let me refer to a book entitled "The Law of Divorce in Canada" by W. Kent Power. He defines general principles not all of them relating to divorce and states:
A person's domicile in the legal sense, except where for some particular purpose the term is defined by statute, is that "country" in which he actually has his permanent home or in which under those principles of private international law which are applied by our courts as part of our law he is deemed to have his permanent home. In respect to domicile in relation to marriage and divorce the nine provinces of Canada are distinct "countries", there is no such thing for the purposes of divorce or the determination of matrimonial status as domicile at large in Canada.
The author then refers to the case of Cook v. Cook, an Alberta case, which he considers to have departed from normal domicile laws. A divorce was granted overlooking certain factors applicable in that province. He then went on to say:
Practical reasons for adopting, by legislation, a Canadian-wide domicile in divorce are the conditions of modern life.
He then says that employees of big corporations who are moved around cannot legitimately claim residence in any province because they may be moved elsewhere at a moment's notice.

Would my hon. friend permit a question. His observations are generally true but does he know of the act passed in 1930 which takes care of cases where women have been deserted by their husbands for more than two years which is true in the present instance?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I will come to that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: What the hon. gentleman is talking about is not applicable.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The hon. member is making a speech from his seat. If he rises I will be seated and listen to him; otherwise I would appreciate his being quiet. The author of this book goes on to say:
If, at some future time which apparently is not yet near, a Canadian divorce law is to be enacted, a statutory change in this rule as to domicile, in so far as it applies to at least eight of the provinces would seem to be logical and desirable.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. We cannot discuss the merits of the divorce act. We

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: must restrict our discussion to the bill before us. What the hon. member is saying has nothing to do with this bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We are not really discussing acts but certain legal terms. The word "domicile" as used in this bill does not relate to any statute.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The only thing we can discuss is what is before us.

May I submit this for consideration. The petition is part of the basis of the bills just as the evidence is part of it. The hon. member seeks to have cleared up the question of domicile. Point No. 3 of the prayer of the petitioner on which the bill is based reads as follows:
3. That at the time of the said marriage your petitioner and the said Charles Edward Vaillan-court were domiciled in Canada, and have ever since continued to be and are now domiciled in Canada, in the province of Quebec.
The fourth paragraph states that the petitioner is residing in the province of Quebec and that the respondent is residing at an address in the city of Winnipeg, Manitoba. We should keep the question of domicile in mind and relate it to the petition which is the reason why we have the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I agree that the hon. member may refer to the question of domicile as it relates to this case but we cannot have a general discussion on divorce legislation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not possible for me to quote the law from memory because I did not study it. I want to point out only that these things have been done in the past, but we do not appear to have jurisdiction to make changes in what is considered to be a mere definition of the statute of domicile. We are now obviously departing from what is considered to be regular domicile. I was going to point out that on occasion courts have made some difference, and one of them was in the passing of the Divorce Jurisdiction Act of 1930. If we are not allowed to go into that, then we wish to say that normally the domicile of the husband is the domicile of the wife. If the wife is living in Quebec and the husband is living in Manitoba, then under the normal domicile procedure she is domiciled in the province of Manitoba although she is actually resident in Quebec. Her domicile will be that of her husband in Manitoba, although she has not seen him for a number of years.
With respect to divorce jurisdiction law, in the case of Cook v. Cook it was said that this principle did not apply to other things than desertion, and that a person
Private Bills-Divorce
could sue for maintenance although the domicile of the wife might be different from the domicile of the husband. If we allow this it will create a great number of problems. I would like to quote from "Fourth (Cumulative) Supplement to Power on Divorce", which was published in 1957. At page 91 under section 73, "Change of Domicile", the following is recited:
P. 297 (e) (Man.) in White v. White, ante, sec. 70, the court held that it was relevant to consider that the plaintiff had left his domicile of origin (Ontario) to avoid complying with an order for maintenance, to evade arrest for such failure, and to seek a divorce where, for lack of funds, his wife would probably be unable to defend the action: White v. White (No. 2) (1950) 2 WWR 687, 59 Man R 181 (1950 ) 4 DLR-[DOT]
I wish they would write these legal documents in English rather than in a lot of other languages.
That is the best remark you have made all day.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I will not cite the rest of it; I do not want to discuss the case, anyway.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: What is the hon. gentleman trying to prove?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am trying to prove that normally this divorce could not be granted because of the two statements that are completely contradictory. In the prayer it is stated that the domicile-and I will read it again:
That at the time of the said marriage your petitioner and the said Charles Edward Vaillancourt were domiciled in Canada, and have ever since continued to be and are now domiciled in Canada, in the province of Quebec.
I maintain this statement in the prayer is absolutely untrue. I was informed by the sponsor the other day that if the various sections of the prayer were not correct then, by law, the divorce could not be granted.

Excuse me; I do not want to take violent exception to that, but I suppose I should raise a question of privilege here. I cannot recall ever making a statement such as that to my hon. friend, but I think he has made some excellent points and probably this petition should have been amended to clear them up. I cannot allow him to say that I told him that if the petition was defective the divorce could not be granted.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I certainly do not want to do any injustice to my hon. friend and I will accept that correction. I would point out that I did ask about a particular section in the petition of a previous bill of a similar nature, and I believe I was told at that time that if the section of the petition and of the prayer

Private Bills-Divorce
was not as stated, then the divorce should not be granted. I believe that is correct.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the practice in the other place has been that when there is evidence of the bill being at variance with the petition there has been a requirement that the petition be amended and re-served on the respondent and the corespondent.
With regard to this particular case, there is no clear evidence to show that the husband is domiciled in Manitoba, except the fact that he is living there. There is a difference between residence and legal status of domicile; but none the less it should undoubtedly have been made more definite, and I think the petition should have been amended and reserved.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I brought in a copy of the Quebec law reports, because there is a case in those reports that applies; it shows that the Quebec courts have ruled on the matter of domicile as it affects them, but unfortunately it is in French and I cannot read it. We have another argument that was presented-
Will my hon. friend permit a question? If he read it in French he could listen to the simultaneous translation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Since this is a serious matter, I would not want to experiment, but I hope to be able to do it in the near future. I hold in my hand a sheet from Chitty's "Law Journal". It contains an article on divorce under the heading of "Random Notes". It involves a case that was heard in the territorial court of the Northwest Territories. It was the case of Voghell v. Yoghell (1959), and reported at page 290, 30 W.W.R., whatever that means. It refers to one particular case, Mr. Chairman, that I think is important and it says:
The question of domicil bothers him a little but after reviewing a number of the well-known cases on the point he decides that the rule as to jurisdiction lying only in the court of the domicil is judge-made law developed in England and the provinces after 1870 and so not applicable to the Northwest Territories. In any event, he considers that for jurisdiction to vest in the territories court, a Canadian domicil is sufficient because the territories are not an independent and sovereign authority such as a province, and therefore Canadian domicil is all that is necessary.
Mr. Chairman, this may be the way of handling divorces, and we may not have to go under the Napoleonic code in the province of Quebec in the matter of civil action; we may not have to give any consideration to the matter of domicile; but, Mr. Chairman, if we do not, then I would suggest that we must send this back to the Senate to have it amended to make it a correct and factual document. If we want to accept Canadian domicile to be

just that, then we have an obligation to refer this back to the Senate to make it correct.
If we do not it will mean that people will be able to take up domicile wherever they wish and the farther away the better and respondents in these cases will not be able to defend themselves because they will not have the means to travel across the country. A case could arise in the province of Quebec where the husband had gone to British Columbia and the wife would not be able to go to British Columbia to bring action but would be able to bring the case to the House of Commons. There would be too much money involved to warrant her going out to British Columbia.
In this case the husband has gone to Manitoba. I suggest that this is working a hardship on other people in Canada because I am quite sure that some people in Ontario would like to get a nice quiet divorce in the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. We are straying away again. May I ask the hon. member for Timiskaming to come back to the bill. I think we have had quite a full discussion of the question of domicile, to which I said he could refer, and I am sure he has made his point.

I wonder whether I could make a very brief observation? The points are very well presented and I can see that the C.C.F. will soon have its own junior lawyer just as the Liberals have in the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. The point is that divorce is a matter of federal jurisdiction under the British North America Act, which has been almost lost sight of in the last couple of weeks, and that it is the practice for the clerks in the other place and the members in the other place to limit cases for hearing to persons whose domicile is shown to be in the province of Newfoundland or the province of Quebec.
This is a rather difficult type of case because the husband deserted the wife and moved to another province. It brought into play, I would think, the federal act of 1930. But I think it should be known that under the law we can deal with cases from any part of Canada we wish. However, it has become the practice to confine cases to these two particular provinces. This is one of these more or less borderline cases that are rather difficult to explain.

This is rather important and I should like to ask a question. The law on divorce is federal but other provinces, with the exception of Newfoundland and Quebec, have accepted jurisdiction in the handling of divorce cases. I could not quite get the point

of the hon. member. The divorce law is federal but in this instance the jurisdiction is federal because two provinces will not accept their jurisdictional responsibilities. What was the point? I am sorry, but I did not get it.

I simply pointed out that under the British North America Act divorce and marriage are matters of federal jurisdiction and the solemnization of marriage is a matter of provincial jurisdiction. If the hon. member wants further information, the authority to grant divorce is exercised-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I think this discussion has gone quite far afield. I should like to remind hon. members again that we have Bill No. SD-29 before us and I would suggest that they keep their remarks relevant to it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to comment on your ruling because it seems to me that most of the bills that come before us as members of parliament are not bills on which we have to express a judicial point of view. But in this case we are all going to have to become lawyers because our set-up is not such that these bills are subjected to the same legal requirements as other bills coming before the house. I submit that all this information is very necessary because we are going to hear a great deal more about these divorces. We are actually dealing with bills that have not had the normal judicial examination. We are really handling court cases.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I must remind the hon. member that I do not make legal rulings.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You will have to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I am sorry, but I do not make legal rulings. I merely follow the rules set down by this house. This, of course, brings me to standing order 59, subsection 4 of which reads as follows:
The chairman Shalt maintain order in the committees of the whole house, deciding all questions of order subject to an appeal to the house.
Subsection 2 reads as follows:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
The Chair cannot go any further than that.
Do you accept divorce bills as being in the same position as any other private bill and open to the same discussion?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Anything can be discussed on a private bill that is relevant to the bill. The question of the evidence has been discussed, and I am not too sure
Business of the House
that everything in the evidence would be relevant to the bill. That is for this committee to decide. But these bills can be discussed individually. It does not make any difference as long as the discussion is relevant to the bill.

This is the point I am trying to get at. The evidence we have on each one of these bills, and I refer particularly now to the bill before us, is evidence taken before the Senate committee and that evidence can be used in the discussion of these bills.

May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I inquire what the business is for next week?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Next week we will start off on Monday and Tuesday with a supply motion.
May I ask if the minister has any information as to the subject of the supply motion?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I would not mind hearing what it will be myself. Then I have a list of eight items of business, the order of which will be determined as the week progresses. I am referring to business for Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. Three of these are motions which refer certain matters to committees and if they are passed quickly by the house it will assist the committees to carry on their studies. One is a motion in the name of the Acting Secretary of State to refer the Canada Elections Act and other matters-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What number?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
-to the committee on privileges and elections. It is No. 18 on the order paper. Then there is a motion which is under government notices of motion today in the name of the Minister of Transport to establish a committee on railways, air lines and shipping. It is important that this committee be set up because the heads of the organizations, the C.N.R., Trans-Canada Air Lines and so on, will be in Ottawa on Tuesday, the 29th, I believe, to appear before the committee.
Third on the list is a motion in my own name, which is found in Votes and Proceedings and will be on the order paper on Monday, to refer to the committee on agriculture and colonization a study of the delivery of grain to feed mills. This will give that committee some work which they

Business of the House
are urgently asking for. I hope to have before the house next week certain amendments affecting the national energy board and if they are on the order paper I would ask the house to consider them before the end of the week.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would that be No. 4?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That would be No. 4 but they will not necessarily be taken up in this order. We have as a fifth item interim supply which will come before the house on Wednesday of next week. As a sixth item we have final supplementary estimates. In case those matters are all concluded before the end of the week, we shall have again before us the resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport concerning amendments to the Railway Act which has been announced previously and has been taken up previously. There is also a resolution in the name of the Minister of Public Works concerning the Trans-Canada Highway Act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: From this list it does not appear as though we shall come back to the tax-sharing agreement next week.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I doubt very much whether we would be able to get to that matter but I will put it as No. 9 in case some of these things are passed rather quickly by the house. The order in which these items will appear I will endeavour to place before the house on Monday night.

May I ask the house leader whether there is any arrangement between the government and the official opposition that on motions of reference there shall be a wide-open debate or whether it shall be restricted to the terms of the resolutions themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No arrangement has been made.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: It being three minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
